question: Avery attacks with a [Guile] that was turned face-down by [Ixidron], and Nelson blocks with [Jerrard of the Closed Fist]. Does Avery shuffle?
answer:
Yes — Avery shuffles Guile into their library.

Why: while turned face down by Ixidron, Guile is a 2/2 creature with no name, no text, no subtypes, no mana cost, and therefore no abilities [Ixidron ruling #4]. That means the face-down Guile does not have "can't be blocked except by three or more creatures," so Nelson's single blocker Jerrard of the Closed Fist can legally block it. Jerrard of the Closed Fist is a 6/5 and deals 6 damage to the 2/2 face-down Guile, which is lethal, so Guile is destroyed and put into its owner's graveyard.

Once in the graveyard, the card is no longer a face-down permanent — it exists as the card Guile, with its abilities. Guile's last ability is worded to trigger when it's put into a graveyard from anywhere, and it triggers from the graveyard itself rather than as a leaves-the-battlefield ability [Guile ruling #0] [Guile ruling #5]. The relevant test is whether the object had the ability at the moment it arrived in the graveyard, not whether it had the ability on the battlefield: an effect that strips the ability while it's on the battlefield still leaves the trigger intact, while something that strips the ability in the graveyard (e.g., Yixlid Jailer) would stop it [Guile ruling #7]. Since Ixidron's effect only applies to the permanent on the battlefield, Guile has its ability in the graveyard, the trigger goes on the stack, and on resolution Avery shuffles Guile into their library.

One caveat on timing: if Guile were somehow moved out of the graveyard after the trigger but before it resolves, it stays where it is and Avery just shuffles their library [Guile ruling #2].

This result is the same whether the game has two players or more — nothing here depends on the number of opponents.

gold_text.603.6c: Trigger events that involve objects changing zones are called “zone-change triggers.” Many abilities with zone-change triggers attempt to do something to that object after it changes zones. During resolution, these abilities look for the object in the zone that it moved to. If the object is unable to be found in the zone it went to, the part of the ability attempting to do something to the object will fail to do anything. The ability could be unable to find the object because the object never entered the specified zone, because it left the zone before the ability resolved, or because it is in a zone that is hidden from a player, such as a library or an opponent’s hand. (This rule applies even if the object leaves the zone and returns again before the ability resolves.) The most common zone-change triggers are enters-the-battlefield triggers and leaves-the-battlefield triggers. Leaves-the-battlefield abilities trigger when a permanent moves from the battlefield to another zone, or when a phased-in permanent leaves the game because its owner leaves the game. These are written as, but aren’t limited to, “When [this object] leaves the battlefield, . . .” or “Whenever [something] is put into a graveyard from the battlefield, . . . .” (See also rule 603.10.) An ability that attempts to do something to the card that left the battlefield checks for it only in the first zone that it went to. An ability that triggers when a card is put into a certain zone “from anywhere” is never treated as a leaves-the-battlefield ability, even if an object is put into that zone from the battlefield.

answer_gold:
Yes. By default, triggered abilities are checked immediately after the event in question to see if they should trigger. At that point, the Guile is face-up in the graveyard and has that ability.

(Guile's trigger does not fit the exception for "leaves-the-battlefield" triggers because it is a "from anywhere" trigger.)

question: Archer attacks with a [The Scarab God] that was turned face-down by [Ixidron] and Nia blocks with [Scathe Zombies]. Does The Scarab God trigger?
answer:
No. While The Scarab God is face down, it has no abilities at all, so nothing triggers — not its death trigger and not its upkeep trigger.

Why: a creature turned face down by Ixidron is a 2/2 creature with no text, no name, no subtypes, and no mana cost [Ixidron ruling #4]. "No text" means the face-down The Scarab God has lost "When The Scarab God dies, return it to its owner's hand at the beginning of the next end step" as well as its upkeep trigger and its activated ability. So when the face-down The Scarab God (a 2/2) trades with Nia's blocking Scathe Zombies (a 2/2) and both die, there is no death trigger and The Scarab God stays in Archer's graveyard (turned face up there, since it's no longer on the battlefield).

Also note Ixidron's own power/toughness is the number of face-down creatures on the battlefield, so if the face-down The Scarab God dies, Ixidron shrinks by one.

I'm assuming The Scarab God was already face down before attackers were declared; that's fine — only a creature can attack, and a face-down The Scarab God is still a creature [506.3]. In a two-player game the nonactive player Nia is the defending player and may be attacked [506.2]. If instead The Scarab God somehow became face up before it died (for example by being turned face up), it would have its abilities again at that time and its death trigger would work normally.

Multiplayer caveat: with more than two players, who Archer may attack depends on the variant's range/attack-direction rules [801.3], but that doesn't change the answer about triggering.

question: Alaia casts [Biogenic Upgrade] targeting [Michelangelo, Weirdness to 11]. In total how many counters are be placed on Michelangelo, Weirdness to 11?
answer:
Nine +1/+1 counters total end up on Michelangelo, Weirdness to 11 (it becomes a 10/10).

Step by step:

1. Distribution: Biogenic Upgrade distributes all three +1/+1 counters to its single target, Michelangelo, Weirdness to 11 (each target must get at least one counter — [Biogenic Upgrade ruling #0]). Michelangelo, Weirdness to 11's own static ability ("If one or more +1/+1 counters would be put on a creature you control, that many plus one are put on it instead") replaces that with 3 + 1 = 4 counters. Michelangelo, Weirdness to 11 is a creature Alaia controls, so it boosts counters put on itself.

2. Doubling: Biogenic Upgrade then doubles the number of +1/+1 counters on Michelangelo, Weirdness to 11. Doubling means putting a number of +1/+1 counters on it equal to the number it already has ([Biogenic Upgrade ruling #2]) — that's 4 counters being put on it. Michelangelo, Weirdness to 11's replacement effect applies again to this new event: 4 + 1 = 5 counters.

Total counters placed: 4 + 5 = 9, so Michelangelo, Weirdness to 11 (a 1/1 base) ends up 10/10.

Notes: Because only one counter-modifying effect (Michelangelo, Weirdness to 11's own) applies to each event here, there's no ordering decision to make; if there were multiple such effects, Alaia would choose the order ([Michelangelo, Weirdness to 11 ruling #1], and generally the affected object's controller chooses which replacement effect to apply first under [616.1] / [616.1e]). If Alaia controlled a second Michelangelo, Weirdness to 11, each would add one more counter per event ([Michelangelo, Weirdness to 11 ruling #3]). Nothing here depends on the number of players.

gold_text.614.1a: Some continuous effects are replacement effects. Like prevention effects (see rule 615), replacement effects apply continuously as events happen—they aren’t locked in ahead of time. Such effects watch for a particular event that would happen and completely or partially replace that event with a different event. They act like “shields” around whatever they’re affecting. Effects that use the word “instead” are replacement effects. Most replacement effects use the word “instead” to indicate what events will be replaced with other events.

If two or more players have to make these choices at the same time, choices are made in APNAP order (see rule 101.4).

If two or more players have to make these choices at the same time, choices are made in APNAP order (see rule 101.4). Any of the applicable replacement and/or prevention effects may be chosen.

answer_gold: Nine. Michelangelo, Weirdness to 11's ability is a replacement effect that applies whenever counters are being placed on it When Biogenic Upgrade begins resolving, that replacement effect will add a counter, resulting in Alaia placing four +1/+1 counters. Afterwards, Biogenic Upgrade will then double the amount of counters on Michelangelo, Weirdness to 11. This results in an additional four counters being placed on it, which will then be modified by Michelangelo, Weirdness to 11's replacement effect again, resulting in nine +1/+1 counters in total.

question: Addison casts [Ferocious Zheng]. After it resolves, they cast [Elemental Eruption] and reveal [Everdream] from their hand, splicing it onto Elemental Eruption. When Elemental Eruption's Storm trigger resolves, will the copies of Elemental Eruption also have Everdream spliced onto them?
answer:
Yes — each storm copy of Elemental Eruption will also have Everdream spliced onto it, so each copy creates a 4/4 red Dragon Elemental token with flying and prowess and then draws Addison a card.

Why: splice onto instant or sorcery is a choice made as you cast the spell (you reveal Everdream from hand and pay its splice cost {2}{U} while casting Elemental Eruption), and when a spell is copied, the choices made while casting it are copied — so the copy has the same spliced-on abilities as the original [Everdream ruling #4]. The spliced effect (drawing a card) happens last, after Elemental Eruption's own effect of creating the token [Everdream ruling #1].

Note you don't pay Everdream's splice cost again for the copies; the copies are put directly onto the stack and aren't cast [Elemental Eruption ruling #2].

On how many copies: Ferocious Zheng was cast before Elemental Eruption this turn, so storm counts it — with just those two spells you get one copy (plus the original), each with Everdream spliced on. Spells that were countered or cast from other zones would also be counted [Elemental Eruption ruling #1]. Each copy can be countered individually, and countering the original Elemental Eruption doesn't affect the copies [Elemental Eruption ruling #0]. Note also that Everdream itself stays in your hand — splicing never puts it on the stack, and if Elemental Eruption were countered it would remain in hand [Everdream ruling #0]. None of this changes between a two-player and a multiplayer game.

question: Nova controls a [Torsten Von Ursus] enchanted by their [Felidar Umbra]. Allen activates the last ability of [Sorin, Lord of Innistrad], targeting the Torsten Von Ursus. What happens?
answer:
Torsten Von Ursus survives. Felidar Umbra's umbra armor replaces the destruction: instead of Torsten Von Ursus being destroyed, all damage is removed from Torsten Von Ursus and Felidar Umbra is destroyed. Umbra armor means "If enchanted creature would be destroyed, instead remove all damage from it and destroy this Aura" — that replacement is mandatory and applies no matter why the creature would be destroyed, including a "destroy" effect like Sorin, Lord of Innistrad's −6 [Felidar Umbra ruling #3][Felidar Umbra ruling #5]. Torsten Von Ursus is not tapped and is not removed from combat, since umbra armor is not regeneration [Felidar Umbra ruling #6].

Because Torsten Von Ursus was never put into a graveyard, Sorin, Lord of Innistrad's "Return each card put into a graveyard this way to the battlefield under your control" does not apply to Torsten Von Ursus — Nova keeps it.

Felidar Umbra, however, is destroyed by Sorin, Lord of Innistrad's ability itself: when a spell or ability would destroy the enchanted creature, that spell or ability is what destroys the Aura instead; umbra armor merely changes the effect [Felidar Umbra ruling #7]. So Felidar Umbra is a card put into a graveyard by Sorin, Lord of Innistrad's ability, and Allen returns Felidar Umbra to the battlefield under Allen's control (Allen would have to attach it to a legal creature; the provided rules don't cover the details of an Aura entering the battlefield this way, so that part isn't fully settled by the context here). Any other creatures/planeswalkers targeted by the same activation are destroyed normally and, if they were cards, returned under Allen's control.

Note also that Sorin, Lord of Innistrad's ability targets; if Torsten Von Ursus somehow gained indestructible, umbra armor would do nothing because nothing would be destroyed [Felidar Umbra ruling #9]. This analysis is the same whether the game has two players or more; nothing here depends on player count.

If an Aura is entering the battlefield under a player’s control by any means other than by resolving as an Aura spell, and the effect putting it onto the battlefield doesn’t specify the object or player the Aura will enchant, that player chooses what it will enchant as the Aura enters the battlefield. The player must choose a legal object or player according to the Aura’s enchant ability and any other applicable effects.

answer_gold: The Felidar Umbra is destroyed instead of the Torsten Von Ursus. It is then returned to the battlefield by the rest of Sorin, Lord of Innistrad's ability. The only creature on the battlefield is the Torsten Von Ursus, so the Felidar Umbra must enter the battlefield enchanting the Torsten Von Ursus. Felidar Umbra is now controlled by Allen.

question: Nico controls [Containment Priest]. Alma attempts to play [Dryad Arbor], which is exiled. Can Alma now play [Sequestered Stash] as their land for turn?
answer:
No. Alma has already used their one land play for the turn on Dryad Arbor, so they can't also play Sequestered Stash (absent an effect granting additional land plays).

Why: Dryad Arbor is a land creature that is played as a land — it doesn't use the stack, isn't a spell, can't be responded to, and it counts as your land play for the turn [Dryad Arbor ruling #4]. Because playing a land isn't casting a spell, Dryad Arbor is a nontoken creature entering the battlefield without having been cast, so Nico's Containment Priest replacement effect exiles it instead (Containment Priest: "If a nontoken creature would enter and it wasn't cast, exile it instead."; [Containment Priest ruling #1] confirms the ability only spares creatures that were actually cast). The land play was still made — the exile replaces the entering event, not the act of playing the land — so the play for the turn is spent and Sequestered Stash stays in hand.

This is the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table: Containment Priest affects any player's uncast nontoken creatures, and each player still gets only their own one land play per turn.

To play a land, a player puts that land onto the battlefield from the zone it was in (usually that player’s hand). By default, a player can take this action only once during each of their turns. A player can take this action any time they have priority and the stack is empty during a main phase of their turn. See rule 305, “Lands.”

answer_gold: No. Regardless of what zone Dryad Arbor moved to, it was still played as Alma's land play, and Alma can only play one land each turn.

question: Norah controls [Blood Sun]. Ari plays [Dark Depths] and then destroys the Blood Sun with [Sultai Charm]. What happens?
answer:
Ari gets Marit Lage. Dark Depths enters the battlefield with zero ice counters on it (because Blood Sun stripped the counter-placing ability), and as soon as Sultai Charm destroys Blood Sun, Dark Depths gets its abilities back, its state trigger immediately sees no ice counters, and Ari sacrifices Dark Depths to create Marit Lage, a legendary 20/20 black Avatar creature token with flying and indestructible.

Step by step:

1. Blood Sun says "All lands lose all abilities except mana abilities." "Dark Depths enters with ten ice counters on it" is an ability that modifies how it enters, and Blood Sun removes it before it applies [Blood Sun ruling #5]. So Dark Depths enters with no ice counters. Note Dark Depths has no mana ability at all, so nothing of it survives Blood Sun [Dark Depths ruling #0].
2. While Blood Sun is on the battlefield, Dark Depths also lacks its state-triggered ability, so nothing triggers even though it has zero counters.
3. Sultai Charm's second mode, "Destroy target artifact or enchantment," legally targets Blood Sun (an enchantment). Once Blood Sun leaves the battlefield, its continuous effect ends and Dark Depths again has its printed abilities [Blood Sun ruling #4 confirms the interaction is about which abilities exist while Blood Sun is out].
4. "When Dark Depths has no ice counters on it, sacrifice it..." is a state trigger, so it triggers immediately upon the condition being true with the ability present [Dark Depths ruling #1]. It resolves, Ari sacrifices Dark Depths, and creates the Marit Lage token. If something bounces or otherwise removes Dark Depths from the battlefield before that trigger resolves, Ari can't sacrifice it and gets no token [Dark Depths ruling #2].

Timing assumption: I'm assuming Dark Depths entered while Blood Sun was already on the battlefield, as stated. If instead Blood Sun had entered after Dark Depths, the ten ice counters would already be there and Ari would still need to pay {3} ten times to remove them.

This interaction doesn't depend on player count — it works the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table, since Sultai Charm just targets Norah's Blood Sun.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).

gold_text.614.12: Some replacement effects modify how a permanent enters the battlefield. (See rules 614.1c–d.) Such effects may come from the permanent itself if they affect only that permanent (as opposed to a general subset of permanents that includes it). They may also come from other sources. To determine which replacement effects apply and how they apply, check the characteristics of the permanent as it would exist on the battlefield, taking into account replacement effects that have already modified how it enters the battlefield (see rule 616.1), continuous effects from the permanent’s own static abilities that would apply to it once it’s on the battlefield, and continuous effects that already exist and would apply to the permanent. Voice of All says “As this creature enters, choose a color” and “This creature has protection from the chosen color.” An effect creates a token that’s a copy of Voice of All. As that token is created, the token’s controller chooses a color for it. Yixlid Jailer says “Cards in graveyards lose all abilities.” Scarwood Treefolk says “This creature enters tapped.” A Scarwood Treefolk that’s put onto the battlefield from a graveyard enters the battlefield tapped. Orb of Dreams is an artifact that says “Permanents enter tapped.” It won’t affect itself, so Orb of Dreams enters the battlefield untapped.

answer_gold: Dark Depths entered the battlefield with no ice counters, since it didn't have the ability that would cause it to enter with them. When Blood Sun is destroyed, Dark Depths triggers since it has no ice counters on it and creates a Marit Lage token.

question: Aiden controls [Volrath's Shapeshifter] and [Yixlid Jailer]. The top card of their graveyard is [Mistform Skyreaver]. Does Volrath's Shapeshifter have flying?
answer:
Yes — Volrath's Shapeshifter has flying (and is a 6/6 Illusion named Mistform Skyreaver with the {1}: change creature type ability, plus its own granted "{2}: Discard a card").

Why: Yixlid Jailer says "Cards in graveyards lose all abilities," so the Mistform Skyreaver card sitting in Aiden's graveyard has no abilities of its own while it's there. But Volrath's Shapeshifter's ability is its own ability functioning on the battlefield, and it's a text-changing effect [Volrath's Shapeshifter ruling #5] that gives Volrath's Shapeshifter "the full text of that card" — its name, mana cost, color, types, abilities, power, and toughness [Volrath's Shapeshifter ruling #1]. Yixlid Jailer doesn't edit the text of the card in the graveyard; it only stops that card's abilities from functioning there. Once that text is copied onto Volrath's Shapeshifter, which is on the battlefield, the abilities work normally — the same principle Yixlid Jailer's own rulings use, where what matters is that the card has the ability on the battlefield [Yixlid Jailer ruling #3]. Card text (Volrath's Shapeshifter's text-copying ability) is what's doing the work here, so it wins over any general expectation that Yixlid Jailer blanks everything about the graveyard card.

Also note Volrath's Shapeshifter keeps the granted "{2}: Discard a card" ability in addition to the copied abilities [Volrath's Shapeshifter ruling #1], and no "enters" abilities trigger when it changes form [Volrath's Shapeshifter ruling #4].

Where Yixlid Jailer would matter: an ability that only functions from the graveyard — e.g. scavenge [702.97a], embalm [702.128a], or eternalize [702.129a] — would be shut off for the card in the graveyard itself, since those abilities function only while the card is in a graveyard [113.6m].

This works the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table; nothing here depends on the number of players.

question: Autumn controls [Bridge from Below] and [Silvercoat Lion]. They cast [Hour of Revelation]. Do they create a Zombie token?
answer:
No — Autumn does not create a Zombie token.

Bridge from Below only functions from a graveyard; while Bridge from Below is on the battlefield it has no effect at all [Bridge from Below ruling #1]. Hour of Revelation destroys all nonland permanents, so Bridge from Below and Silvercoat Lion are both destroyed and put into Autumn's graveyard at the same time. For Bridge from Below's first ability to trigger on Silvercoat Lion dying, Bridge from Below must already be in the graveyard immediately before Silvercoat Lion dies; since Bridge from Below was still on the battlefield at that moment and only arrives in the graveyard simultaneously with Silvercoat Lion, the ability doesn't trigger at all [Bridge from Below ruling #0].

Note also that Hour of Revelation destroys all nonland permanents — opponents' creatures too. But that's irrelevant here for the same reason: Bridge from Below wasn't in the graveyard before those deaths either, so its second (exile) ability doesn't trigger. This works the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table, since Hour of Revelation hits every player's nonland permanents and Bridge from Below cares only about which graveyard a creature is put into, not who controlled it [Bridge from Below ruling #3].

Cost note, for completeness: Hour of Revelation costs {3}{W}{W}{W}, and if there are ten or more nonland permanents on the battlefield when Autumn casts it, the {3} generic portion is reduced to nothing, leaving {W}{W}{W}; the three white symbols are never reduced [Hour of Revelation ruling #0].

If instead Bridge from Below had already been in Autumn's graveyard when Hour of Revelation resolved, Silvercoat Lion's death would trigger the first ability and Autumn would get a 2/2 black Zombie token.

answer_gold: No. Leaves-the-battlefield triggers care about the state of the game immediately before the event in question. Bridge from Below was on the battlefield at that time, and won't trigger.

question: Axl activates [Ring of Ma'rûf]'s ability in their upkeep. What happens in Axl's draw step if they don't own any cards outside the game?
answer:
Short answer: Axl draws no card in their draw step. Ring of Ma'rûf's ability says "The next time you would draw a card this turn, instead put a card you own from outside the game into your hand." That replaces the draw step draw. Since Axl owns no cards outside the game, there's nothing to put into their hand, so the draw is simply replaced by nothing — Axl gets no card at all, and the replacement is used up.

A note on timing: I'm assuming Axl activated the ability before the draw step (during the beginning phase of their own turn), so the draw step draw is the "next time you would draw a card this turn." If some earlier draw had already occurred after activation (for example from another effect), that earlier draw would have been the one replaced and the draw step draw would happen normally.

Also relevant from the card's own ruling: Ring of Ma'rûf doesn't just hand you a card — it only functions as a draw replacement, and if you wouldn't draw a card during the rest of the turn the ability has no effect at all [Ring of Ma'rûf ruling #0]. Note that {5} in its activation cost is generic mana (payable with mana of any color or colorless), and {T} means tapping it; the ability also exiles Ring of Ma'rûf itself, so it's gone from the battlefield either way.

The rules excerpts provided here cover phasing and turn-based actions rather than draw replacement, so this answer rests on Ring of Ma'rûf's printed text and its ruling. Nothing here depends on the number of players, so the result is the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table.

Such effects watch for a particular event that would happen and completely or partially replace that event with a different event. They act like “shields” around whatever they’re affecting. Effects that use the word “instead” are replacement effects. Most replacement effects use the word “instead” to indicate what events will be replaced with other events.

answer_gold: Axl is required to attempt to find a card from outside the game, if they fail to find one, then when the ability resolves they will put nothing into their hand. Since Ring of Ma'rûf sets up a replacement effect, Axl can't choose to ignore it.

question: Athena control [Krark, the Thumbless] and [Spark Double] copying it. They cast [Song of Totentanz], which triggers both Krark, the Thumbless. When the first trigger resolves they lose the flip and return Song of Totentanz to hand. What happens when the second trigger resolves?
answer:
The second Krark, the Thumbless trigger (the one from Spark Double, which is a non-legendary copy of Krark, the Thumbless) still resolves normally, and you still flip a coin.

- If you win that flip, a copy of Song of Totentanz is created on the stack even though Song of Totentanz itself is no longer there [Krark, the Thumbless ruling #12]. That copy keeps the value of X chosen as Song of Totentanz was cast [Krark, the Thumbless ruling #3], so it creates that many 1/1 black Rat tokens with "This token can't block" and gives creatures you control haste when it resolves. The copy isn't cast, so cast-triggers (including Krark's own) don't trigger again [Krark, the Thumbless ruling #2].
- If you lose that flip, nothing is returned to your hand — Song of Totentanz has already left the stack and stays in its current zone (your hand) [Krark, the Thumbless ruling #4].

Background: both triggers went on the stack together and are independent; losing the first flip removed Song of Totentanz from the stack without countering it [Krark, the Thumbless ruling #14], but that does not remove or invalidate the second trigger [Krark, the Thumbless ruling #1]. Spark Double copies Krark, the Thumbless exactly except that it isn't legendary, so it genuinely has the same triggered ability [Spark Double ruling #6].

Assumption on timing: I'm assuming the first trigger fully resolved (returning Song of Totentanz to hand) before the second trigger resolved. If you had instead ordered them so the winning flip resolved first, that copy would resolve before Song of Totentanz [Krark, the Thumbless ruling #15], and Song of Totentanz could then still be returned by the later losing flip. None of this depends on player count — it plays out the same in two-player and multiplayer games.

question: Alden cast [Ixidron]. Natalie controls a very cute [Tangled Florahedron]. What happens to it?
answer:
Natalie's Tangled Florahedron is turned face down as Ixidron enters, becoming a nameless 2/2 creature with no text — so it loses its "{T}: Add {G}" mana ability.

Details:

- Ixidron's own text says "As this creature enters, turn all other nontoken creatures face down." Tangled Florahedron on the battlefield (front face up, a 1/1 Elemental creature) is another nontoken creature, so it's turned face down.
- Turned-down creatures are 2/2 creatures with no text, no name, no subtypes, no expansion symbol, and no mana cost, and those are the copiable values while it's face down [Ixidron ruling #4]. Its normal characteristics aren't copiable during that time.
- This happens *as* Ixidron enters, so there is never a moment with Ixidron on the battlefield and Tangled Florahedron face up; "whenever another creature enters" abilities won't see a face-up Tangled Florahedron [Ixidron ruling #3]. Note the exception: if Tangled Florahedron were entering the battlefield at the same time as Ixidron, it would enter face up instead [Ixidron ruling #1].
- Natalie may look at her face-down Tangled Florahedron at any time; Alden may not, but all players must be able to keep track of which face-down permanent is which [Ixidron ruling #2].
- Ixidron's power/toughness equal the number of face-down creatures on the battlefield, so Natalie's face-down Tangled Florahedron counts toward that.

A caution: the provided rules and card data don't include the specific rules for a modal double-faced card being turned face down (nothing in the context addresses whether an MDFC can be turned face down or how its back face, Tangled Vale, interacts). I'm answering from Ixidron's text and rulings, which straightforwardly cover "all other nontoken creatures." Nothing here changes based on player count — Ixidron affects every other nontoken creature regardless of controller, so the same thing happens in a two-player or multiplayer game.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).

gold_text.712.16: Melded permanents and other double-faced permanents can’t be turned face down. If a spell or ability tries to turn a double-faced permanent face down, nothing happens and that effect doesn’t change any of its characteristics or their copiable values.

answer_gold: Nothing. Tangled Florahedron cannot be turned face down.

question: Amani controls [Leyline of the Void] and casts [Hypnotic Cloud] to have Nicolas discard a card. Nicolas discards [Loxodon Smiter]. Does it end up on the battlefield or in exile?
answer:
Loxodon Smiter ends up on the battlefield, assuming Nicolas (the card's owner/the affected player) applies Loxodon Smiter's own replacement effect.

Why: Hypnotic Cloud makes Nicolas discard a card, and discarding normally puts the card into Nicolas's graveyard. Two replacement effects want to change that same event:
- Leyline of the Void (controlled by Amani): "If a card would be put into an opponent's graveyard from anywhere, exile it instead."
- Loxodon Smiter's own text: "If a spell or ability an opponent controls causes you to discard this card, put it onto the battlefield instead of putting it into your graveyard." Hypnotic Cloud is a spell an opponent (Amani) controls, so this condition is met. This printed card text is what overrides the ordinary "discarded cards go to the graveyard" outcome.

Only one of the two can apply, because each replaces the same graveyard-bound event. Once Loxodon Smiter's effect is applied, the card never would be put into Nicolas's graveyard, so Leyline of the Void's exile replacement has nothing left to replace and Loxodon Smiter enters the battlefield under Nicolas's control. (If instead Leyline of the Void's effect were applied first, the card would be exiled and Loxodon Smiter's effect would then have nothing to replace.)

Caveat on grounding: the rules excerpts provided here do not include the rule that says which player chooses the order when multiple replacement effects would apply to the same event (that is normally the affected object's controller/owner, here Nicolas). So the tie-break choice is not something I can cite from the given context — I'm noting that as the missing piece. Nicolas will naturally choose Loxodon Smiter's effect, putting it onto the battlefield.

Also note: Nicolas has still discarded a card, so discard-triggered abilities trigger either way [Loxodon Smiter ruling #0]. And Loxodon Smiter arrives with summoning sickness — it can't attack or use {T}/{Q} abilities until it has been under Nicolas's control since the start of his most recent turn [302.6]. This analysis is the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table; Leyline of the Void applies to each of its controller's opponents, and Loxodon Smiter only cares that the discard came from a spell an opponent controls.

question: In a Commander game with 4 players, Ari casts [Kardur, Doomscourge]. Bode controls [Oxidda Finisher], and [Parhelion II], which is not a creature at the time Kardur, Doomscourge's enter the battlefield ability resolves. During Bode's next turn, can they attack Ari with Parhelion II? Can they have the Angel tokens created by Parhelion II attack Ari?
answer:
Short answer: No to Parhelion II (if it's a creature when attackers are declared, it must attack someone other than Ari), and yes to the Angel tokens — Bode may have them attacking Ari.

Parhelion II: Kardur, Doomscourge's first ability applies to "creatures your opponents control" for the duration (until Ari's next turn), and it isn't limited to creatures present when it resolved — per [Kardur, Doomscourge ruling #2] it also affects creatures that come under an opponent's control later. So once Bode crews Parhelion II and it becomes an artifact creature during Bode's turn, Parhelion II is subject to both requirements: it attacks each combat if able, and it attacks a player other than Ari if able. With four players there are two other opponents available, so Parhelion II must be declared as attacking one of those other players (or an opposing planeswalker) — Bode chooses which, per [Kardur, Doomscourge ruling #3]. Only if Parhelion II could not legally attack any player other than Ari would it be required/allowed to attack Ari instead ([Kardur, Doomscourge ruling #0]). In a two-player game the "other than you" clause would have no other player to satisfy, so Parhelion II would attack Ari — that difference is exactly why the 4-player table matters here. Note also that if Bode never crews Parhelion II, it isn't a creature and simply doesn't attack; Kardur, Doomscourge's requirement never forces Bode to pay a crew cost ([Kardur, Doomscourge ruling #4]).

The Angel tokens: Parhelion II's triggered ability creates two 4/4 Angels that are already attacking, and Bode chooses which players or planeswalkers each token is attacking ([Parhelion II ruling #0]). Those tokens were never declared as attacking creatures ([Parhelion II ruling #1]), so the declare-attackers requirement imposed by Kardur, Doomscourge — which constrains how attackers are declared — never applies to them. Bode may put both Angels in as attacking Ari.

Oxidda Finisher, for completeness: it's a creature Bode controls, so if it's able to attack it must attack, and must attack a player other than Ari if able — meaning it goes at one of the other two opponents.

Timing assumption: I'm assuming Parhelion II is crewed before the declare attackers step of Bode's turn and that Bode's turn falls before Ari's next turn (so Kardur, Doomscourge's effect is still active). If instead Ari's next turn has already begun, the effect has expired and Bode is free to attack Ari with Parhelion II normally.

Similarly, if an effect states that a creature is attacking, its controller chooses which defending player, planeswalker a defending player controls, or battle a defending player protects it’s attacking (unless the effect has already specified). Such creatures are “attacking” but, for the purposes of trigger events and effects, they never “attacked.” They remain attacking creatures until they’re removed from combat or the combat phase ends, whichever comes first.

A continuous effect generated by the resolution of a spell or ability that doesn’t modify the characteristics or change the controller of any objects modifies the rules of the game, so it can affect objects that weren’t affected when that continuous effect began. If a single continuous effect has parts that modify the characteristics or changes the controller of any objects and other parts that don’t, the set of objects each part applies to is determined independently. Bode cannot attack Ari with Parhelion II, but they can choose for the Angel tokens to attack Ari.

Kardur, Doomscourge's enters-the-battlefield ability sets up a rules change that causes any creatures Ari's opponents control to have to attack if able and to have to attack another player if able. Since this is a change in the rules of the game, it affects Parhelion II even if it is not a creature at the time the ability resolves.

The Angel tokens are created attacking, but are never declared as attackers. Because of this, Bode can choose Ari to be the defending player for the tokens.

question: Aislinn controls two [Bramblewood Paragon]s and casts [Thunder-Thrash Elder]. What is the maximum amount of counters Thunder-Thrash Elder can enter the battlefield with?
answer:
Direct answer: with only the two Bramblewood Paragons on the battlefield, Thunder-Thrash Elder can enter with at most 8 +1/+1 counters — 6 from Devour 3 (sacrificing both Bramblewood Paragons: 3 × 2) plus 2 from the two Bramblewood Paragons' entry bonus. If Aislinn controls other creatures too, the maximum is 3 × (number of creatures sacrificed) + 2.

How the pieces work:

- Thunder-Thrash Elder is a Lizard Warrior, so each Bramblewood Paragon applies "Each other Warrior creature you control enters with an additional +1/+1 counter on it." Two Bramblewood Paragons stack, giving +2 counters [Bramblewood Paragon ruling #1], and this stacks on top of whatever counters Devour 3 would otherwise give [Bramblewood Paragon ruling #2].
- Devour 3 lets Aislinn sacrifice any number of creatures already on the battlefield as Thunder-Thrash Elder enters; it enters with three times that many counters. Thunder-Thrash Elder cannot devour itself, and cannot devour creatures entering at the same time as it [Thunder-Thrash Elder ruling #0]. The choice of how many and which creatures to sacrifice is made during resolution of Thunder-Thrash Elder [Thunder-Thrash Elder ruling #1].

Assumption and caveat: I'm assuming the only creatures Aislinn controls are the two Bramblewood Paragons, which is why the answer is 8. Note that both effects (Devour's sacrifice and the Bramblewood Paragon counter bonus) are applied as Thunder-Thrash Elder enters, so the two Bramblewood Paragons are still there when their replacement effects are applied — hence the +2 still counts even though they are the creatures devoured. The provided rules context does not include the layered replacement-effect rules (614.x) that would let me demonstrate that ordering from a numbered rule, so treat that specific point as the standard reading rather than something I can cite here. If Aislinn instead sacrificed creatures other than the Bramblewood Paragons, the +2 is unambiguous and the total is 3 × (creatures sacrificed) + 2.

This answer doesn't depend on player count; it's the same in two-player and multiplayer games.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).

Such effects watch for a particular event that would happen and completely or partially replace that event with a different event. They act like “shields” around whatever they’re affecting. Effects that read “[This permanent] enters with . . . ,” “As [this permanent] enters . . . ,” or “[This permanent] enters as . . . “ are replacement effects.

answer_gold: Eight. Both Bramblewood Paragon and Thunder-Thrash Elder have replacement effects that modify how Thunder-Thrash Elder enters the battlefield. While Thunder-Thrash Elder is entering the battlefield the game checks which replacement effects to apply, and sees that there are two Bramblewood Paragons that want to place an additional +1/+1 counter on Thunder-Thrash Elder as well as a Devour ability. If Aislinn chooses to devour the Bramblewood Paragons, they will place an additional six +1/+1 counters on Thunder-Thrash Elder.

question: Is [Umori, the Collector] a legal companion for a deck containing only [Grist, the Hunger Tide], creatures, and lands?
answer:
Yes. Umori, the Collector is a legal companion for that deck. Umori's companion requirement is that each nonland card in your starting deck shares a card type [Umori, the Collector ruling #1]. Grist, the Hunger Tide has the ability "As long as Grist isn't on the battlefield, it's a 1/1 Insect creature in addition to its other types," and this applies in deck construction and in every zone other than the battlefield — anywhere but the battlefield Grist, the Hunger Tide is a Legendary Planeswalker Creature — Grist Insect [Grist, the Hunger Tide ruling #3], and that ability works before the game begins during deck construction [Grist, the Hunger Tide ruling #2]. So Grist, the Hunger Tide shares the card type "creature" with all the other nonland cards, and the requirement is met. Note this is Grist, the Hunger Tide's own printed text creating the extra type, which is why it counts as a creature card even though it's also a planeswalker card.

Details worth knowing:
- Land cards are ignored entirely for the requirement, and they may have any number of extra types [Umori, the Collector ruling #4].
- Umori, the Collector itself is your companion, so it starts outside the game (your sideboard) and is not part of your starting deck, so its own types don't matter for the check [Umori, the Collector ruling #0], [Umori, the Collector ruling #11].
- Once the game begins, you may pay {3} as a special action, any time you could cast a sorcery, to put Umori, the Collector from outside the game into your hand; it can't be responded to [Umori, the Collector ruling #15], [Umori, the Collector ruling #9].
- If you choose "creature" as Umori, the Collector's chosen type on the battlefield, Grist, the Hunger Tide cast as a spell is a creature spell (it's not on the battlefield while on the stack), so it would cost {1} less — but only generic mana is reduced, so {1}{B}{G} becomes just {B}{G} [Umori, the Collector ruling #5].
- Multiplayer note: nothing here changes with player count, except that if several players want to reveal a companion, the starting player reveals first and the rest follow in turn order [Umori, the Collector ruling #2]. In Commander, your commander must also meet the requirement, and your companion isn't one of your 100 cards [Umori, the Collector ruling #7].

Abilities of all other objects usually function only while that object is on the battlefield. The exceptions are as follows: An ability that states which zones it doesn’t function in functions everywhere except for the specified zones, even outside the game and before the game begins.

answer_gold: Yes. Grist, the Hunger Tide's ability is in effect even before the game begins..

question: Abel crews their [Adrestia]. Nathalie activates their [Mobilized District] causing it to become a creature. After that resolves, Nathalie casts [Mirrorweave] targeting their Mobilized District. What are Adrestia's characteristics after Mirrorweave resolves?
answer:
After Mirrorweave resolves, Adrestia is no longer a creature at all — it becomes a nonlegendary land named Mobilized District with no power or toughness.

Why: Mirrorweave says "Each other creature becomes a copy of target nonlegendary creature until end of turn." Because Abel crewed Adrestia, Adrestia was an artifact creature (Vehicle) at that moment, so it is one of the "other creature[s]" affected. The copy only picks up the printed values of Nathalie's Mobilized District plus copy effects on it — not the ability-generated effect that animated Mobilized District into a 3/3 Citizen with vigilance [Mirrorweave ruling #0]. This is exactly the Mutavault example: targeting an animated land copies only the printed wording, so the other creatures become unanimated lands [Mirrorweave ruling #5].

So Adrestia's characteristics become: name Mobilized District, no mana cost (mana value 0), colorless, card type Land only (it loses Artifact, Vehicle, and the Legendary supertype, plus Islandwalk, its attack trigger, and Crew 1), no power/toughness, and it has the abilities "{T}: Add {C}" and "{4}: This land becomes a 3/3 Citizen creature with vigilance until end of turn. It's still a land. This ability costs {1} less to activate for each legendary creature and planeswalker you control." Note that {C} is colorless mana specifically, and the {4} is generic mana reduced only in its generic portion; a legendary planeswalker that's also a creature reduces it by only {1} [Mobilized District ruling #0]. It is still controlled by Abel and is still tapped if crewing/attacking left it tapped.

Because Adrestia is no longer a creature, it can't be declared as an attacker, so its "Whenever Adrestia attacks, if an Assassin crewed it this turn" trigger is moot — that trigger would only have applied if the crewing creature was an Assassin when it was tapped to pay Crew [Adrestia ruling #2]. At end of turn, Mirrorweave's effect wears off and Adrestia reverts to its own characteristics [Mirrorweave ruling #3]; the crew effect (which also lasts until end of turn) will have expired by then too.

Timing note: I'm assuming the animation of Mobilized District had already resolved before Mirrorweave was cast, as stated. That order doesn't change the outcome — Mirrorweave never copies the animation effect either way.

This answer doesn't depend on the number of players; it works the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table, except that Mirrorweave affects every other creature on the battlefield, including those controlled by additional opponents.

question: Ari controls a [Lunarch Inquisitors] that exiled a [Jasmine Boreal] when it transformed. Nyla casts [Moonmist]. Does the Jasmine Boreal return to the battlefield?
answer:
No — Jasmine Boreal stays in exile. Moonmist transforms all Humans, so Ari's Lunarch Inquisitors (a Human Cleric on a double-faced card) turns back into Avacynian Missionaries. But transforming back is not the same as leaving the battlefield: the exile effect lasts "until this creature leaves the battlefield," and the permanent is still on the battlefield, just with its other face up. Per the card's ruling, if Lunarch Inquisitors somehow transforms into Avacynian Missionaries, the exiled creature remains exiled; it will only return if Avacynian Missionaries later leaves the battlefield [Avacynian Missionaries // Lunarch Inquisitors ruling #5].

Two side notes: Jasmine Boreal itself is a Human, but Moonmist only transforms permanents on the battlefield and only double-faced cards can transform at all, so nothing happens to it in exile. Also, once Avacynian Missionaries is equipped again at the beginning of Ari's end step it will transform back into Lunarch Inquisitors, and that new transform triggers the "When this creature transforms into Lunarch Inquisitors" ability again, potentially exiling another target creature — the still-exiled Jasmine Boreal is unaffected by that. Moonmist's damage prevention is irrelevant here. Nothing about this changes between a two-player game and a multiplayer table, except that if Ari (the owner of Lunarch Inquisitors) leaves a multiplayer game, the exiled Jasmine Boreal returns to the battlefield [Avacynian Missionaries // Lunarch Inquisitors ruling #3].

question: Addison controls [Carth the Lion] and [Bioessence Hydra]. Addison activates the [+1] ability of [Dovin, Architect of Law]. How many times does Bioessence Hydra trigger?
answer:
Bioessence Hydra triggers once, and that single trigger puts two +1/+1 counters on Bioessence Hydra.

Why: Carth the Lion says "Planeswalkers' loyalty abilities you activate cost an additional [+1] to activate," so the [+1] ability of Dovin, Architect of Law costs [+2] instead ([Carth the Lion ruling #3]). The cost is calculated first and paid as a single action, so two loyalty counters are put on Dovin, Architect of Law at one time rather than one at a time ([Carth the Lion ruling #0]).

Bioessence Hydra's ability reads "Whenever one or more loyalty counters are put on planeswalkers you control, put that many +1/+1 counters on this creature." Because it triggers on "one or more" counters at once, the two counters on Dovin, Architect of Law cause exactly one trigger, which puts two +1/+1 counters on Bioessence Hydra.

Note also that this is the activation cost being paid; the ability's own effect (gain 2 life, draw a card) doesn't add further loyalty counters. If Addison controlled two Carth the Lion effects, the cost would instead be [+3] and Bioessence Hydra would still trigger once, for three +1/+1 counters ([Carth the Lion ruling #1]). Nothing here depends on the number of players.

question: Nico casts [Assert Authority] targeting Ainsley's [Blightsteel Colossus]. What happens as Assert Authority resolves?
answer:
Blightsteel Colossus is countered and goes to exile — it does not get shuffled back into Ainsley's library.

As Assert Authority resolves, it counters Blightsteel Colossus, and because Assert Authority says "If that spell is countered this way, exile it instead of putting it into its owner's graveyard," the countered Blightsteel Colossus card is put into the exile zone rather than the graveyard. Blightsteel Colossus's own replacement effect reads "If Blightsteel Colossus would be put into a graveyard from anywhere, reveal Blightsteel Colossus and shuffle it into its owner's library instead." That effect only applies to an event of being put into a graveyard. Since Assert Authority has already replaced the graveyard destination with exile, Blightsteel Colossus is never put into a graveyard, so its shuffle-back ability never applies. This is a case of specific card text (Assert Authority's exile clause) determining the outcome over the general "countered spells go to the graveyard" result.

Exile and the graveyard are distinct zones, so Blightsteel Colossus sits in exile, out of Ainsley's library and unreachable by its own shuffle effect.

On cost: Assert Authority costs {5}{U}{U}, and affinity for artifacts reduces only the generic portion — with, say, three artifacts you'd pay {2}{U}{U}; the two {U} symbols can never be reduced.

This answer is the same whether the game has two players or more than two; only Nico (the caster) and Ainsley (the spell's owner) are involved, and the card goes to exile regardless of table size.

What I can't ground in the given context: whether Amani, who is at 3 life and takes 3 damage, is still around to discard and make the copy, and what happens to the copy once Amani loses the game. None of those rules were provided here, so I won't guess at them.

Also note the context I was given on simultaneous choices is APNAP-based (rule 101.4/101.4c) and applies to multiple players choosing at once; it doesn't govern this single-player choice, and nothing here changes based on whether the game has two players or more than two — though if there are more than two players, Campbell being a third player is exactly the case Chain of Plasma's "may choose a new target" clause allows.

question: Aspen attacks with [Hammers of Moradin]. During the combat damage step, they use [Time Stop] to end the turn. What happens to the tokens created by myriad?
answer:
The myriad tokens stay on the battlefield — they are not exiled. Time Stop's "end the turn" effect removes all attacking and blocking creatures (including Hammers of Moradin and its myriad tokens) from combat, then skips straight to the cleanup step [Time Stop ruling #3]. Because the game never reaches an end of combat step, the myriad delayed trigger "Exile the tokens at end of combat" never gets a chance to trigger, so the token copies of Hammers of Moradin simply remain in play (untapped-status unchanged, no longer attacking). Nothing in the end-the-turn process puts that ability on the stack: state-based actions are checked, but no player gets priority and no triggered abilities are put onto the stack [724.1c], [Time Stop ruling #3]. If some ability had actually triggered during the process, it would be put on the stack during the cleanup step, giving players a chance to respond and causing an extra cleanup step [Time Stop ruling #2] — but the myriad exile ability isn't one of them here.

Also note the tokens themselves were never declared as attackers, so they never had triggers of their own to worry about [Hammers of Moradin ruling #5].

Multiplayer note: this scenario only arises at a table with more than two players. If Aspen's defending player were their only opponent, myriad would create no tokens at all [Hammers of Moradin ruling #3], and one token is created for each opponent other than the defending player.

Timing assumption: I'm assuming Time Stop resolved during the combat damage step, before the end of combat step began, as stated. If instead Time Stop resolved after the end of combat step had already begun and the myriad delayed ability had already resolved, the tokens would already be exiled and Time Stop would change nothing about them.

question: If Avery is going first, they'd like to reveal [Umori, the Collector] as their companion. If they're going second, they don't want to have a companion. Can they do this?
answer:
Yes. The decision to reveal a companion is made before decks are shuffled into libraries, at which point the starting player has already been determined, so Avery may reveal Umori, the Collector as their companion when they're going first and decline to reveal any companion when they're going second. [Umori, the Collector ruling #8]

Details:
- Before shuffling your deck to become your library, you may reveal one card from outside the game (your sideboard in tournament play) as your companion, provided your starting deck meets the companion requirement. You may not reveal more than one, and it stays revealed outside the game as the game begins. [Umori, the Collector ruling #8], [Umori, the Collector ruling #0]
- Revealing is optional, so choosing not to reveal when going second is entirely legal. But once Avery has chosen not to reveal a companion, they can't change their mind later in that game. [Umori, the Collector ruling #2]
- Umori, the Collector's requirement is that each nonland card in Avery's starting deck shares a card type; that requirement applies only to the starting deck, not the sideboard, and lands may have any extra types. Declining to reveal doesn't change deck legality either way, since the companion isn't one of the cards in the starting deck. [Umori, the Collector ruling #1], [Umori, the Collector ruling #11], [Umori, the Collector ruling #4], [Umori, the Collector ruling #6]
- Multiplayer note: the same answer holds with more than two players. If multiple players want to reveal companions, the starting player reveals first and the rest proceed in turn order — so Avery still knows their seat/turn position when deciding, though they will see fewer or more other players' reveals depending on where they sit. [Umori, the Collector ruling #2]

Once the game is underway, if Avery did reveal Umori, the Collector, they may pay {3} as a special action any time they could cast a sorcery (main phase, stack empty, they have priority) to put it into their hand; that action doesn't use the stack and can't be responded to. [Umori, the Collector ruling #9], [Umori, the Collector ruling #15]

question: Aspen casts [Greater Good] sacrificing their [Bane Alley Blackguard] which is enchanted with [Mystic Subdual]. How many cards do they draw?
answer:
Aspen draws zero cards, then still discards three cards (or their whole hand if fewer than three).

Why: Bane Alley Blackguard is a 1/3. Mystic Subdual gives the enchanted creature -2/-0 and makes it lose all abilities, so while enchanted Bane Alley Blackguard is a -1/3. Greater Good's ability draws cards equal to the sacrificed creature's power as it last existed on the battlefield [Greater Good ruling #0], which was -1 — you can't draw a negative number of cards, so no cards are drawn. The discard is not optional or conditional on the draw, so Aspen then discards three cards; with fewer than three in hand, they discard their hand [Greater Good ruling #1]. All of this happens during the resolution of Greater Good's ability, so no player can act between the draw and the discard [Greater Good ruling #2].

One wording note: Greater Good is an enchantment ({2}{G}{G}) with the activated ability "Sacrifice a creature: Draw cards equal to the sacrificed creature's power, then discard three cards." You don't sacrifice as part of casting it — Greater Good must already be on the battlefield and the sacrifice is the ability's cost. I'm assuming Mystic Subdual was still attached at the moment Bane Alley Blackguard was sacrificed; if Mystic Subdual had already left the battlefield first, Bane Alley Blackguard's last existing power would have been 1 and Aspen would draw one card, then discard three.

This answer doesn't depend on player count, so it's the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table.

question: Ari controls [Mana Reflection] and [Looming Spires]. Nicole controls [Damping Sphere]. If Ari taps the Looming Spires for mana, how much mana is produced, and of what type(s)?
answer:
Ari gets a single {C} (one colorless mana) — not {R}{R}, and not two colorless.

Why: tapping Looming Spires for mana would normally add {R}. Two replacement effects want to modify that mana event, and when multiple replacement effects would modify mana an ability produces, you choose one to apply, then check whether any others are now applicable; a replacement effect can't apply to the same event twice ([Damping Sphere ruling #2]).

- Damping Sphere's first ability only applies "if a land is tapped for two or more mana." At the moment Looming Spires is tapped it would produce just one mana, so Damping Sphere isn't applicable yet.
- So Mana Reflection applies: Ari is tapping a permanent for mana (activating a mana ability with {T} in its cost — [Mana Reflection ruling #3]), so Looming Spires produces twice as much of that mana, i.e. {R}{R}.
- Now Looming Spires has been tapped for two mana, so Damping Sphere is applicable and replaces that: it "produces {C} instead of any other type and amount." That wording replaces both the type and the amount, so the result is exactly one {C}, not {C}{C}.

Note {C} is colorless mana specifically; it can pay generic costs like {1} but cannot pay a {R} in a cost.

This result doesn't depend on the number of players — Damping Sphere affects any land tapped for two or more mana regardless of who controls it, so it's the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table.

One ordering caveat: if you tried to apply Damping Sphere first, it simply wouldn't be applicable (only one mana at that point), so the sequence above is the only legal one and the answer doesn't change.

A player controls two permanents, each with an ability that reads “If a creature you control would deal damage to a permanent or player, it deals double that damage to that permanent or player instead.” A creature that normally deals 2 damage will deal 8 damage—not just 4, and not an infinite amount.

question: Natasha and Nico are playing Two-Headed Giant, and each controls their own copy of [Bloodbond Vampire]. Ariel controls [Wall of Shards], and on their next upkeep they put the third age counter on it. Can Ariel have Natasha gain one life and Nico gain two? If so, how many triggered abilities of Bloodbond Vampire will be put on the stack?
answer:
Yes, and the total is three Bloodbond Vampire triggers.

How the payment works: with the third age counter on Wall of Shards, Ariel must pay its cumulative upkeep cost three times — that is, "an opponent gains 1 life" three times — or sacrifice Wall of Shards; partial payment isn't allowed [Wall of Shards ruling #1]. Ariel may choose a different opponent for each age counter, or the same opponent more than once [Wall of Shards ruling #0]. So Ariel can name Natasha for one instance and Nico for the other two, which leaves Natasha having gained 1 life and Nico having gained 2 life in total (as two separate 1-life events, not one 2-life event).

How the triggers count: Bloodbond Vampire triggers once for each life-gaining event, regardless of the amount [Bloodbond Vampire ruling #0]. Natasha gaining 1 life is one event, and Nico's two payments are two separate events. Natasha's own Bloodbond Vampire triggers once (from her 1 life); Nico's own Bloodbond Vampire triggers twice (from the two separate 1-life gains). In Two-Headed Giant, life gained by a teammate does not trigger your Bloodbond Vampire even though the team's life total goes up [Bloodbond Vampire ruling #1], so Natasha's copy doesn't see Nico's gains and Nico's copy doesn't see Natasha's gain. Three triggered abilities go on the stack, each putting a +1/+1 counter on its own Bloodbond Vampire.

Assumption on sequencing: I'm treating the three cost payments as three distinct life-gaining events, which is why Nico's copy triggers twice rather than once. If instead Ariel had somehow caused a single event in which Nico gained 2 life at once, Nico's Bloodbond Vampire would trigger only once and the total would be two triggers.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).

gold_text.702.24a: Cumulative Upkeep Cumulative upkeep is a triggered ability that imposes an increasing cost on a permanent. “Cumulative upkeep [cost]” means “At the beginning of your upkeep, if this permanent is on the battlefield, put an age counter on this permanent. Then you may pay [cost] for each age counter on it. If you don’t, sacrifice it.” If [cost] has choices associated with it, each choice is made separately for each age counter, then either the entire set of costs is paid, or none of them is paid. Partial payments aren’t allowed. A creature has “Cumulative upkeep {W} or {U}” and two age counters on it. When its ability next triggers and resolves, the creature’s controller puts an age counter on it and then may pay {W}{W}{W}, {W}{W}{U}, {W}{U}{U}, or {U}{U}{U} to keep the creature on the battlefield. A creature has “Cumulative upkeep—Sacrifice a creature” and one age counter on it. When its ability next triggers and resolves, its controller can’t choose the same creature to sacrifice twice. Either two different creatures must be sacrificed, or the creature with cumulative upkeep must be sacrificed.
gold_text.810.9: Damage, loss of life, and gaining life happen to each player individually. The result is applied to the team’s shared life total. In a Two-Headed Giant game, a player casts Flame Rift, which reads, “Flame Rift deals 4 damage to each player.” Each team is dealt a total of 8 damage.

answer_gold: Paying Wall of Shards' cumulative upkeep involves the choice of an opponent. The choice for each age counter is made individually, then the whole cost is paid at once. This means Ariel can make the stated choice, and the result of this is Natasha gains one life and Nico gains two life. Because of this, each player's Bloodbond Vampire will trigger separately, causing two instances of the triggered ability to be put on the stack. Although the players share a life total, gaining life happens to each player individually.

question: Nataly controls [Urza's Saga] with 2 lore counters on it. Alex casts [Magus of the Moon]. What does Urza's Saga look like?
answer:
Urza's Saga becomes an Enchantment Land — Saga Mountain with no chapter abilities and no {T}: Add {C} ability — just "{T}: Add {R}" — and because it's still a Saga with no chapter abilities, Nataly must sacrifice it immediately.

Details:
- Magus of the Moon's static ability "Nonbasic lands are Mountains" applies to Urza's Saga. Urza's Saga loses its other land types (including the Urza's Saga land type) and all of its abilities, and gains the type Mountain plus "{T}: Add {R}" [Magus of the Moon ruling #4].
- That means Urza's Saga loses its three chapter abilities, and also loses any ability it had gained from chapters I and II (the "{T}: Add {C}" ability and the "{2}, {T}: create a Construct token" ability), even though it normally keeps those for as long as it's on the battlefield [Urza's Saga ruling #5].
- Magus of the Moon does not remove the enchantment card type or the Saga subtype, and it doesn't change names or supertypes [Magus of the Moon ruling #1]. So it's still a Saga sitting there with 2 lore counters and zero chapter abilities.
- A Saga with no chapter abilities is sacrificed immediately as a state-based action, so Nataly sacrifices Urza's Saga right away — she never gets chapter III [Urza's Saga ruling #1].

Note: Urza's Saga's lore counters and its third chapter don't get a chance to trigger later, and even if Magus of the Moon somehow lost its abilities afterward, the type-changing effect would still apply [Magus of the Moon ruling #0].

This works the same regardless of the number of players at the table; Magus of the Moon affects all nonbasic lands, so every opponent's nonbasic lands (not just Nataly's) become Mountains.

question: Niko controls [Metallurgeon] and [Ornithopter of Paradise]. Avery casts [Prismari Command], choosing the "deal 2 damage" and "destroy target artifact" modes, targeting Ornithopter of Paradise with both. In response, Niko activates Metallurgeon's ability targeting Ornithopter of Paradise. What happens?
answer:
Short answer: the provided rules don't include the regeneration or lethal-damage rules needed to settle this definitively, so I can't fully resolve it without guessing.

What the provided material does support: Metallurgeon's ability ({W}, {T}: Regenerate target artifact) legally targets Ornithopter of Paradise, since Ornithopter of Paradise is an artifact creature, and it resolves before Prismari Command because it was activated in response. Prismari Command then resolves with both chosen modes still pointing at Ornithopter of Paradise; because at least one target is still legal, Prismari Command resolves and does as much as it can (Prismari Command ruling #0), applying its modes in the order printed on the card — the 2-damage mode, then the destroy-artifact mode. Only if every target were illegal would Prismari Command do nothing at all (Prismari Command ruling #1).

What's missing from the context: the rule defining what a regeneration shield does (that it's a replacement effect which replaces a destruction event by tapping the permanent, removing it from combat, and removing all damage marked on it), and the state-based-action rule that destroys a creature with lethal damage marked on it. Both are needed to say whether the single regeneration shield is consumed by the destroy-artifact mode or by the 2 damage marked on Ornithopter of Paradise (a 0/2), and therefore whether Ornithopter of Paradise survives.

Timing note: I'm assuming Niko's Metallurgeon activation resolves fully before Prismari Command, as stated. If instead Prismari Command had already resolved before Metallurgeon's ability was activated, there would be nothing to regenerate — Ornithopter of Paradise would already have left the battlefield, and Metallurgeon's ability would have no legal target.

This analysis doesn't depend on player count; it works the same in a two-player or multiplayer game.

question: Ahmed controls [Bronze Sable]. They cast [Genesis Wave], putting [Phylactery Lich] and [Solemnity] onto the battlefield. Does Bronze Sable get a phylactery counter?
answer:
No — Bronze Sable does not get a phylactery counter, and Ahmed will have to sacrifice Phylactery Lich.

Why: All permanents put onto the battlefield by Genesis Wave enter at the same time ([Genesis Wave ruling #5]), so Solemnity is already on the battlefield and its continuous effects are in force at the moment Phylactery Lich's "As this creature enters, put a phylactery counter on an artifact you control" replacement effect is applied. Solemnity says "Counters can't be put on artifacts, creatures, enchantments, or lands," and it stops counters from being put on such a permanent both as it enters and later ([Solemnity ruling #8]). Bronze Sable is an artifact creature already on the battlefield, so the phylactery counter simply can't be put on it.

The exception in [Solemnity ruling #6] does not help here: that ruling only covers a permanent that would enter the battlefield with counters on itself at the same time Solemnity enters. Bronze Sable is not entering — it's an existing permanent receiving a counter from Phylactery Lich's ability — so Solemnity's prohibition applies normally.

Consequence: with no counter placed, Phylactery Lich's first ability accomplishes nothing, and its last ability — a state trigger — triggers immediately because Ahmed controls no permanents with phylactery counters, forcing him to sacrifice Phylactery Lich ([Phylactery Lich ruling #0], [Phylactery Lich ruling #2]). If the ability is somehow countered while the condition remains true, it triggers again ([Phylactery Lich ruling #2]).

Note on ordering: I'm assuming Solemnity and Phylactery Lich hit the battlefield together off the same Genesis Wave, which is what the question describes. If instead Phylactery Lich had entered earlier (before Solemnity was on the battlefield), the counter would have been placed on Bronze Sable at that time and Solemnity wouldn't remove it ([Solemnity ruling #0]), so Phylactery Lich would survive.

Nothing here depends on player count, so the answer is the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).

answer_gold: Yes. Phylactery Lich and Solemnity enter the battlefield at the same time. Solemnity's effect must exist before Phylactery Lich enters the battlefield in order to prevent Bronze Sable from getting a counter.

question: Ashley controls [Tatterkite]. Ashley casts [Genesis Wave], putting [Phylactery Lich] and [Humility] onto the battlefield. Can they put a phylactery counter on Tatterkite?
answer:
No. Tatterkite says "This creature can't have counters put on it," and that card text overrides the general effect of Phylactery Lich's enters-the-battlefield ability. A spell or ability that would put a counter on Tatterkite simply doesn't affect it — the ability isn't countered, the counter just never goes on [Tatterkite ruling #1] [Tatterkite ruling #2]. So Ashley can't choose Tatterkite to receive the phylactery counter.

What Ashley must do instead: Phylactery Lich's ability requires choosing an artifact Ashley controls that is already on the battlefield — permanents entering at the same time off Genesis Wave aren't eligible [Phylactery Lich ruling #1] [Genesis Wave ruling #5]. If Tatterkite is Ashley's only artifact already on the battlefield, no phylactery counter is placed at all, and the ability simply does nothing [Phylactery Lich ruling #0].

The Humility wrinkle: Humility makes all creatures lose all abilities and be 1/1 [Humility ruling #1]. Since Humility entered simultaneously with Phylactery Lich, once both are on the battlefield Phylactery Lich has no abilities — including its "When you control no permanents with phylactery counters on them, sacrifice this creature" state trigger [Phylactery Lich ruling #2]. With that ability stripped by Humility, there is nothing to trigger, so Phylactery Lich (now a 1/1 with no indestructible) is not sacrificed even though no phylactery counter exists. Note also that Tatterkite becomes a 1/1 and loses flying and its own "can't have counters put on it" ability while Humility is on the battlefield — so counters could be put on Tatterkite from that point forward; the restriction only mattered for the moment Phylactery Lich's as-enters choice was made.

Nothing here depends on the number of players; the answer is the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table.

answer_gold: No. Phylactery Lich and Humility enter the battlefield at the same time. Tatterkite had the ability that prevents it from getting counters immediately before Phylactery Lich entered the battlefield, which is when it matters.

question: Avery controls [The One Ring] and casts [Teferi's Protection] then casts a second The One Ring. What happens at the start of the next turn?
answer:
Direct answer: As Avery's next turn begins, Avery's protection from everything and the "life total can't change" effect from Teferi's Protection both end (they last "until your next turn"), and during Avery's untap step the permanents that phased out — including the first The One Ring — phase back in, with any burden counters they had still on them [Teferi's Protection ruling #15]. Avery then controls two copies of the legendary artifact The One Ring, and the "legend rule" applies: Avery keeps one and puts the other into the graveyard (indestructible does not save it, because the legend rule doesn't destroy). Then, at the beginning of Avery's upkeep, the surviving The One Ring's trigger makes Avery lose 1 life for each burden counter on it, and that life loss now happens normally because the "life total can't change" effect has already ended [Teferi's Protection ruling #21].

Why the second The One Ring could be cast at all: while the first The One Ring was phased out it was treated as though it didn't exist, so it couldn't be targeted, its abilities did nothing, and it wasn't there for the legend rule to see [Teferi's Protection ruling #5]. Teferi's Protection only phases out permanents Avery controlled as it resolved, so the newly cast second The One Ring entered the battlefield normally and, since Avery cast it, gave Avery protection from everything again (redundant with Teferi's Protection).

Timing/ordering note: I'm assuming Teferi's Protection resolved while the first The One Ring was on the battlefield, and the second The One Ring was cast afterward, as stated. Phasing in happens before untap, i.e., at the start of Avery's untap step, so if the "next turn" is an opponent's turn (possible with more than two players), Avery's protection and the life-total lock still end when Avery's next turn begins, but the phased-out The One Ring does not return until Avery's own untap step; nothing about this differs between a two-player and a multiplayer game other than whose turn comes next.

Caveat on grounding: the numbered rules supplied here do not include the text of the legend rule or the phasing rules themselves; that part of the answer rests on the phasing behavior described in the Teferi's Protection rulings plus the legend rule, which isn't quoted in the context.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).

Destruction or removal of the source after that time won’t affect the ability. In these cases, any activated or triggered ability that references information about the source for use while announcing an activated ability or putting a triggered ability on the stack checks that information when the ability is put onto the stack. When the triggers resolve the trigger affiliated with the sacrificed The One Ring will use last known information to determine how many counters were on it, and how much life Avery should lose.

question: Amaya controls [Dralnu, Lich Lord], [Furnace of Rath] and six [Snow-Covered Forest]s. Nico casts [Incinerate] targeting Dralnu, Lich Lord. If Amaya chooses to sacrifice Furnace of Rath, how many other permanents will they need to sacrifice?
answer:
Direct answer: five other permanents (six total, counting Furnace of Rath) — assuming the doubling from Furnace of Rath is applied to the damage event first.

Why: Incinerate would deal 3 damage to Dralnu, Lich Lord. Two replacement effects want to modify that same damage event — Furnace of Rath ("it deals double that damage") and Dralnu, Lich Lord ("If damage would be dealt to Dralnu, sacrifice that many permanents instead"). Because two replacement effects are trying to modify how the event affects Dralnu, Lich Lord, Amaya (the controller of the affected object) chooses the order in which they apply [616.1f], and this matches Furnace of Rath ruling #4.

If Amaya applies Furnace of Rath first, the damage becomes 6, and then Dralnu, Lich Lord's replacement effect makes Amaya sacrifice 6 permanents instead of dealing that damage. Amaya controls 8 permanents (Dralnu, Lich Lord, Furnace of Rath, and six Snow-Covered Forests), so 6 is payable: Furnace of Rath plus 5 others. Sacrificing Furnace of Rath at that point does not undo the doubling, which was already applied to the event. Note Amaya could even include Dralnu, Lich Lord itself among the sacrifices [Dralnu, Lich Lord ruling #4].

Other timing/order reading: if Amaya instead applies Dralnu, Lich Lord's replacement effect first, the 3 damage is replaced by sacrificing 3 permanents; no damage is ever dealt, so Furnace of Rath has nothing left to double, and Amaya would sacrifice Furnace of Rath plus only 2 others. Also, had Dralnu, Lich Lord's damage exceeded Amaya's permanent count, Amaya would simply sacrifice every permanent they control [Dralnu, Lich Lord ruling #13].

Since no damage is actually dealt to Dralnu, Lich Lord, Incinerate's "can't be regenerated" clause never attaches to it. This analysis doesn't depend on player count — it works the same in a two-player or multiplayer game.

question: Aubrey and Arely are playing 2HG. Aubrey attacks with [Coral Commando] and Arely casts [Flash Conscription] to gain control of Coral Commando after it's been declared as an attacker in the declare attackers step. Is it still attacking?
answer:
I can't ground this one in the rules provided. The provided context has nothing about combat, attacking creatures, or what happens when a creature changes controllers mid-combat — the relevant material (the declare attackers step, and the rule about a creature being removed from combat when its controller changes) simply isn't in the excerpts given to me, and the Flash Conscription text/ruling supplied only covers untapping, control until end of turn, haste, and the {W}-kicker lifelink-style trigger.

What I can say from what's here: Flash Conscription reads "Untap target creature and gain control of it until end of turn. That creature gains haste until end of turn," so Arely does become the controller of Coral Commando for the rest of the turn, and the supplied Flash Conscription ruling #0 confirms that if {W} was spent, whoever controls Coral Commando when it deals combat damage is the player who gains the life. Whether Coral Commando is still an attacking creature after that control change is exactly the point the missing combat rules would settle.

Two further notes: this is Two-Headed Giant, and no multiplayer or Two-Headed Giant rules were provided either, so I can't tell you how the team structure (Aubrey and Arely being on the same team, or on opposing teams) affects the attack. If they are teammates, Arely taking control of Coral Commando wouldn't change which team is being attacked; if they are opponents, the defending-player question matters — but again, none of that is in the provided context.

Timing assumption: I'm reading the question as Flash Conscription being cast and resolving during the declare attackers step, after attackers were legally declared. If instead it resolved before attackers were declared, Coral Commando was never an attacker in the first place and the question wouldn't arise.
