question: Nicolas controls [Razorfield Thresher], [Lake of the Dead], and [Veinfire Borderpost]. Aubrey controls [Omniscience] and casts [Casualties of War], choosing Razorfield Thresher as the artifact target and the creature target. Then they cast [Radiate], targeting Casualties of War. What will be destroyed after all spells and abilities have resolved?
answer:
Only Razorfield Thresher is destroyed; Radiate produces no copies (unless some other artifact creature is on the battlefield).

Why:

1. Casualties of War is modal — Aubrey chose the "Destroy target artifact" and "Destroy target creature" modes. Each mode may be chosen only once, but both may point at the same permanent, and Razorfield Thresher is an Artifact Creature — Construct, so it is a legal target for both [Casualties of War ruling #0]. Casting it for free off Omniscience changes nothing about targeting; Omniscience only removes the mana cost.

2. Radiate requires the targeted spell to target "only a single permanent or player." Casualties of War has two targeting instructions, but both point at the same object — Razorfield Thresher — so it targets only a single permanent and Radiate can legally target it.

3. Radiate then copies Casualties of War "for each other permanent or player the spell could target." The copies have the same modes chosen (artifact and creature), so a legal target must be simultaneously an artifact and a creature. Lake of the Dead is a land, Veinfire Borderpost is a noncreature artifact, and Omniscience is an enchantment — none of them can be targeted by both the artifact mode and the creature mode. So there is no "other permanent" the spell could target, and Radiate creates zero copies.

4. Radiate resolves doing nothing, then Casualties of War resolves and destroys Razorfield Thresher (both modes hit the same permanent; destroying it once is all that happens). Any abilities that trigger on its destruction wait until Casualties of War finishes resolving [Casualties of War ruling #1].

Note that Lake of the Dead's sacrifice-a-Swamp clause only matters when it would enter the battlefield [Lake of the Dead ruling #0]; it isn't relevant here.

Multiplayer difference: with more than two players, Radiate would still make a copy for every other artifact creature anywhere on the battlefield, including ones controlled by additional opponents — so if a third player controlled an artifact creature, a copy would be created targeting it and that creature would also be destroyed. With only Nicolas and Aubrey as described, nothing else dies.

question: Alonso controls [Spark Double] and casts [Clone]. Alonso would like to have Clone copy Spark Double, then they would like to apply the replacement effect Clone inherited from Spark Double and have it copy Spark Double again. If Alonso has Clone copy Spark Double a total of four times, how many +1/+1 counters will Clone enter the battlefield with?
answer:
Clone enters the battlefield as a copy of Spark Double with exactly one +1/+1 counter on it — not four. The premise of "copying Spark Double four times" doesn't work.

Why: Clone's ability and Spark Double's ability are both copy effects applied as the permanent enters the battlefield. When Alonso has Clone enter as a copy of Spark Double, Clone gets Spark Double's copiable text, including "You may have this creature enter as a copy of a creature or planeswalker you control... it enters with an additional +1/+1 counter on it if it's a creature." That copy-modification is applied once to the single event of Clone entering; a replacement effect can't be reapplied to the same entering event to re-copy Spark Double over and over, so there is no loop generating extra counters. Note also that if the Spark Double Alonso already controls were itself copying something else, Clone would simply enter as whatever that Spark Double copied [Spark Double ruling #7] [Clone ruling #5]. Here Spark Double is copying nothing, so Clone enters as a plain Spark Double.

The single counter comes from Spark Double's own "enters with an additional +1/+1 counter" clause, which functions on the copy [Spark Double ruling #1] [Spark Double ruling #3] [Clone ruling #2] — that card text is what grants the counter, overriding the fact that Clone itself says nothing about counters. So Clone is on the battlefield as a nonlegendary Spark Double [Spark Double ruling #6] that is a 0/0 with one +1/+1 counter, i.e. a 1/1; if it had instead copied nothing at all it would be a 0/0 and die immediately [Clone ruling #7] [704.5f].

One caveat on grounding: the numbered rule stating that a given replacement effect may modify a particular event only once was not included in the context provided to me, so that part of the reasoning rests on the copy rulings above rather than a quoted rule. Nothing here depends on the number of players — the answer is the same in a two-player or multiplayer game, since Spark Double only ever lets you copy a permanent you control.

answer_gold: One. Spark Double has a copy effect that includes an exception (entering with a +1/+1 counter). If another copy effect is applied afterwards, the exception from the first effect will not happen.

question: Nickolas controls a [Nyx Herald] enchanted by [Drake Umbra]. Ainsley casts [Fracturing Gust]. How much life do they gain?
answer:
Ainsley gains 2 life (assuming Nyx Herald enchanted by Drake Umbra are the only artifacts/enchantments on the battlefield).

Why: Fracturing Gust destroys all artifacts and enchantments. Nyx Herald is an Enchantment Creature, so Fracturing Gust would destroy both Nyx Herald and Drake Umbra at the same time. Drake Umbra has umbra armor: if the enchanted creature would be destroyed, instead remove all damage from it and destroy Drake Umbra. This replacement is mandatory [Drake Umbra ruling #1], and when a single spell would destroy both the Aura and the creature it enchants, umbra armor saves the enchanted creature — Fracturing Gust ends up destroying Drake Umbra "in two different ways at the same time," with the same result as destroying it once [Drake Umbra ruling #4].

So the only permanent actually destroyed here is Drake Umbra. Fracturing Gust's controller (Ainsley) gains 2 life for each permanent destroyed this way, and no life is gained for a permanent that survives [Fracturing Gust ruling #0]. Nyx Herald remains on the battlefield as a 2/3 (it loses the +3/+3 and flying from Drake Umbra). Note the life goes to Ainsley, who cast Fracturing Gust, not to Nickolas.

If there are other artifacts or enchantments on the battlefield (in a two-player or a multiplayer game — Fracturing Gust hits everyone's permanents equally), add 2 life for each of those that's actually destroyed; indestructible ones or ones saved by their own umbra armor don't count.

question: Avery controls [Corpsejack Menace] and casts [Rescuer Sphinx], choosing to return Corpsejack Menace to their hand. How many +1/+1 counters will Rescuer Sphinx enter the battlefield with?
answer:
Rescuer Sphinx enters with just one +1/+1 counter, not two.

Rescuer Sphinx's own text is a replacement effect that applies as it enters: "As this creature enters, you may return a nonland permanent you control to its owner's hand. If you do, this creature enters with a +1/+1 counter on it." Avery chooses Corpsejack Menace as the permanent to return, and that return is carried out as part of Rescuer Sphinx entering the battlefield — no player may take actions between the choice and Rescuer Sphinx being on the battlefield with its +1/+1 counter (Rescuer Sphinx ruling #2).

Corpsejack Menace's ability ("If one or more +1/+1 counters would be put on a creature you control, twice that many +1/+1 counters are put on it instead") does apply to counters a creature enters the battlefield with (Corpsejack Menace ruling #0). But it can only do so if Corpsejack Menace is on the battlefield at the time Rescuer Sphinx enters. Here Corpsejack Menace has already been returned to Avery's hand, so its replacement effect isn't around to modify the event, and Rescuer Sphinx enters with the single counter.

If Avery instead returned some other nonland permanent and left Corpsejack Menace on the battlefield, Rescuer Sphinx would enter with two +1/+1 counters (and with two Corpsejack Menaces, four — Corpsejack Menace ruling #1).

This outcome is the same regardless of the number of players at the table; nothing here depends on opponents.

question: Arabella casts [Mind's Desire]. In response, Neil casts [Lim-Dûl's Vault]. How many copies of Mind's Desire are created when the storm trigger resolves?
answer:
When the storm trigger resolves, Neil's Lim-Dûl's Vault does not add a copy. Storm copies Mind's Desire once for each spell cast *before it* this turn, and Lim-Dûl's Vault was cast after Mind's Desire (in response to it), so it isn't counted. If Arabella's Mind's Desire was the first spell cast that turn, zero copies are created and the storm trigger simply resolves doing nothing; if other spells had already been cast earlier in the turn, the count is that number, still excluding Lim-Dûl's Vault.

Details worth knowing:
- Storm's count includes spells cast from zones other than the hand and spells that were countered [Mind's Desire ruling #3], so anything cast earlier in the turn by any player counts — but only spells cast strictly before Mind's Desire.
- The copies are put directly onto the stack rather than cast [Mind's Desire ruling #4], so they won't be counted by later storm spells, and each copy must be countered individually [Mind's Desire ruling #5]. A copy of a spell isn't cast and copies the original's choices [707.10b].
- The storm triggered ability itself can be countered by effects that counter triggered abilities; if countered, no copies are made [Mind's Desire ruling #2].
- Note that Lim-Dûl's Vault, resolving first, will shuffle and rearrange Neil's own library; it has no effect on Arabella's Mind's Desire, which shuffles Arabella's library and exiles the top card of Arabella's library face up [Mind's Desire ruling #0].

This is the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table: the storm count is of all spells cast before Mind's Desire that turn by any player, and a spell cast in response never counts.

question: Aubrey casts [Bitter Ordeal], targeting Natasha. At their first opportunity, Aubrey sacrifices their [Westvale Abbey]. How many cards will Aubrey be able to exile from Natasha's library?
answer:
Aubrey exiles just one card (assuming no other permanents had already hit a graveyard earlier that turn).

Bitter Ordeal's gravestorm ability reads, "When you cast this spell, copy it for each permanent put into a graveyard this turn." That triggered ability triggers on casting, and it counts the permanents already put into graveyards at the time it resolves. Aubrey's "first opportunity" to sacrifice Westvale Abbey comes only after Bitter Ordeal has already been cast — so Westvale Abbey reaching the graveyard is too late to be counted, and no gravestorm copy is created for it. Aubrey resolves only the original Bitter Ordeal: search Natasha's library for one card and exile it, then Natasha shuffles.

Timing note: I'm assuming the sacrifice happens after Bitter Ordeal is cast (which is what "at their first opportunity" means, since the gravestorm trigger is put on the stack as part of casting). If instead Aubrey had sacrificed Westvale Abbey before casting Bitter Ordeal, gravestorm would have counted it and made one copy, letting Aubrey exile two cards.

Also note Westvale Abbey's own text: its third ability sacrifices five creatures (not the land) to transform it, so if Aubrey used that ability, five creature permanents — not the Abbey — would be the permanents put into a graveyard; done before casting, that would yield five gravestorm copies for six cards exiled total. Done after casting, it still adds nothing.

This answer is the same whether the game has two players or more; Bitter Ordeal simply targets one player, here Natasha.

If the spell has any targets, you may choose new targets for any of the copies.”

answer_gold: 2. Gravestorm cares about the number of permanents put into the graveyard before the trigger resolves.

question: Ainsley activates [Priest of Forgotten Gods]'s ability, but doesn't choose a target for the first part. Can Nickolas respond to the ability?
answer:
Yes. Nickolas can respond. Even with no targets chosen, the ability of Priest of Forgotten Gods is not a mana ability — because it's an ability that may have targets, it uses the stack and can be responded to [Priest of Forgotten Gods ruling #1]. So it goes on the stack, players receive priority, and Nickolas may cast instants or activate abilities in response (for example, removing Priest of Forgotten Gods, though the ability will still resolve and Ainsley will still add {B}{B} and draw a card per [Priest of Forgotten Gods ruling #0]).

This is true regardless of how many players are at the table; nothing here depends on a two-player game.

answer_gold: Yes. One of the qualifications for being a mana ability is that the ability doesn't require a target. Priest of Forgotten Gods's ability is still considered to require targets even if zero targets were chosen for it.

question: Analia controls [Volrath's Shapeshifter] and [Muldrotha, the Gravetide], and the top card of their graveyard is [Grid Monitor]. Can Analia cast the Grid Monitor?
answer:
No — as long as Grid Monitor is the top card of Analia's graveyard, Analia can't cast it.

Why: Volrath's Shapeshifter says that as long as the top card of your graveyard is a creature card, it has the full text of that card. Grid Monitor is a creature card (an Artifact Creature), so Volrath's Shapeshifter has Grid Monitor's name, mana cost, color, types, power/toughness, and abilities — including "You can't cast creature spells" (Volrath's Shapeshifter ruling #1). That static prohibition applies to Analia.

Muldrotha, the Gravetide would otherwise let Analia cast one permanent spell of each permanent type from the graveyard, and Grid Monitor could be announced as either Analia's artifact spell or creature spell for that turn (Muldrotha, the Gravetide rulings #0 and #7). But it doesn't matter which type Analia announces: a "creature spell" is any spell with the type Creature even if it also has another type such as Artifact (Grid Monitor ruling #1), so casting Grid Monitor is casting a creature spell and is prohibited. Muldrotha, the Gravetide only grants timing permission; you must still follow other restrictions (Muldrotha, the Gravetide ruling #5).

The catch-22 is self-reinforcing: the only thing making the restriction exist is Grid Monitor sitting on top of the graveyard, and that is exactly the card Analia wants to cast. Analia can break out of it by using the granted "{2}: Discard a card" ability on Volrath's Shapeshifter (or any other discard/mill) to put a different card on top of the graveyard. If the new top card isn't a creature card, Volrath's Shapeshifter reverts to a 0/1 blue creature with no Grid Monitor text (Volrath's Shapeshifter ruling #0), and Analia may then cast Grid Monitor from the graveyard with Muldrotha, the Gravetide — but only if Grid Monitor is still the appropriate card in the graveyard and Analia hasn't already used that permanent-type slot this turn. Note the discarded card goes on top of the graveyard, so choose a noncreature card.

Also note Analia must still pay Grid Monitor's cost of {4} (four generic mana) when casting it (Muldrotha, the Gravetide ruling #2), and must announce that Muldrotha, the Gravetide is the permission being used (Muldrotha, the Gravetide ruling #1). None of this depends on player count — it's the same in two-player and multiplayer games.

question: Antoine owns an [Eternal Scourge] that was exiled by Nico's [Ixalan's Binding]. Can Antoine cast it?
answer:
No. Antoine can't cast that Eternal Scourge while Nico's Ixalan's Binding keeps it exiled.

Eternal Scourge's own text ("You may cast this card from exile") does give Antoine permission to cast it from the exile zone rather than from his hand, but that permission still requires following normal timing rules and paying its {3} cost [Eternal Scourge ruling #2]. Ixalan's Binding, however, says "Your opponents can't cast spells with the same name as the exiled card." Antoine is an opponent of Nico, the controller of Ixalan's Binding, so he is flatly prohibited from casting a spell named Eternal Scourge — including the exiled card itself, and including any other copy of Eternal Scourge in his hand, graveyard, or library. A card's specific text applies here on both sides: Eternal Scourge grants a casting permission, but Ixalan's Binding imposes a restriction, and a restriction on casting can't be overridden by mere permission.

Multiplayer note: this restriction applies to every opponent of Nico, not just Antoine, so at a larger table no opponent of Nico can cast a spell named Eternal Scourge. Nico himself is unrestricted by his own Ixalan's Binding, but Eternal Scourge's "you may cast this card from exile" refers to its owner/controller, so that doesn't help Nico cast Antoine's card.

If Nico's Ixalan's Binding later leaves the battlefield, the exiled Eternal Scourge card returns to the battlefield immediately under Antoine's control (its owner), with nothing happening in between [Ixalan's Binding ruling #4], and the name restriction ends with it.

question: Avery manifests the top card of their library with [Soul Summons]. Then, they mutate [Trumpeting Gnarr] targeting the manifested creature. What are the characteristics of the resulting creature if Avery chooses to put the manifested creature on top?
answer:
Direct answer: the merged permanent is the face-down manifested card on top, so it's a nameless, colorless 2/2 creature with no card types beyond creature, no creature types, and mana value 0 — but it now also has Trumpeting Gnarr's abilities from underneath: mutate {3}{G/U}{G/U} and "Whenever this creature mutates, create a 3/3 green Beast creature token." That triggered ability triggers from this very mutation, so Avery gets a 3/3 green Beast token.

Details:
- "Manifest" means putting the top card of the library onto the battlefield face down as a 2/2 creature; a face-down manifested permanent is a 2/2 creature with no name, no mana cost, no creature types, and no abilities, is colorless, and has mana value 0 [Soul Summons ruling #8]. Because it has no creature types it isn't Human, so it's a legal target for Trumpeting Gnarr's mutate.
- Mutate as printed on Trumpeting Gnarr: the spell is put over or under the target non-Human creature you own, and "They mutate into the creature on top plus all abilities from under it." With the manifested creature on top, the top card supplies name, power/toughness, color, mana value, types (i.e., the face-down 2/2 profile), and Trumpeting Gnarr supplies only abilities.
- Trumpeting Gnarr's ability is part of the mutating permanent as it mutates, so "Whenever this creature mutates" triggers and creates one 3/3 green Beast creature token.
- Avery can still later turn the face-down card face up for its mana cost if it's a creature card, as a special action any time they have priority; a manifested creature remains turnable face up even after losing abilities [Soul Summons ruling #2, Soul Summons ruling #6]. Doing so changes the characteristics the top card supplies but doesn't cause enters-the-battlefield abilities to trigger and doesn't affect attachments or targeting [Soul Summons ruling #11, Soul Summons ruling #12]. Avery may look at the face-down card at any time [Soul Summons ruling #5], and must reveal it if the permanent leaves the battlefield [Soul Summons ruling #4].

Caveat: the provided context contains no numbered rules for mutate or merged permanents, so the answer above rests on Trumpeting Gnarr's own printed text plus the Soul Summons rulings on face-down/manifested permanents. Nothing here is two-player specific, so it works the same at a multiplayer table.

question: Nayeli controls a [Yixlid Jailer]. Ariel has a [Golgari Brownscale] in their graveyard and returns it to their hand with [Disturbing Plot]. Does Ariel gain 2 life?
answer:
No — Ariel does not gain 2 life.

Yixlid Jailer says "Cards in graveyards lose all abilities." While Golgari Brownscale sits in Ariel's graveyard, it has no abilities at all, including "When this card is put into your hand from your graveyard, you gain 2 life." That ability's trigger event is Golgari Brownscale leaving the graveyard for the hand, so the ability would have to function from the graveyard — exactly the situation Yixlid Jailer shuts off. Compare [Yixlid Jailer ruling #4]: an ability that triggers when the object having it is put into a graveyard from somewhere other than the battlefield triggers from the graveyard, and Yixlid Jailer stops it from triggering at all; the mirror-image case here (triggering as it leaves the graveyard) works the same way, whereas [Yixlid Jailer ruling #6] shows that only abilities whose trigger is checked while the card is in a zone Yixlid Jailer doesn't affect (the battlefield) still work.

So Disturbing Plot resolves, Golgari Brownscale goes from Ariel's graveyard to Ariel's hand, and nothing triggers. Once it's in hand it does have its abilities again, but the trigger event has already passed.

Two notes: (1) I'm assuming Yixlid Jailer was already on the battlefield when Disturbing Plot resolved. If Yixlid Jailer left the battlefield before Disturbing Plot resolved, Golgari Brownscale would have its ability in the graveyard and Ariel would gain 2 life. (2) If Ariel had conspired Disturbing Plot (tapping two untapped black creatures they control) to copy it and returned a second Golgari Brownscale, that copy would likewise cause no life gain while Yixlid Jailer is out. Yixlid Jailer's effect applies regardless of who controls the graveyard, so the answer is the same in a two-player or multiplayer game.

question: Aryana has taken control of an [Ahn-Crop Crasher] from Noe with [Tibalt, the Fiend-Blooded], which Aryana exerts. After Aryana ends their turn, will it untap during Noe's untap step?
answer:
Yes. Ahn-Crop Crasher will untap normally during Noe's untap step.

Exert means you choose, as you declare the creature as an attacker, to get a bonus effect at the cost of that creature not untapping during its controller's next untap step ([Ahn-Crop Crasher ruling #1] confirms exert is chosen at declare-attackers). Tibalt, the Fiend-Blooded's −6 ability gains control of creatures only until end of turn, so Aryana's control of Ahn-Crop Crasher ends when the turn ends and the card returns to Noe's control.

Exert's "won't untap during your next untap step" refers to the untap step of the player who exerted it — Aryana. Since Ahn-Crop Crasher is back under Noe's control, Noe's untap step untaps it normally; the exert restriction would only have mattered in Aryana's next untap step, by which time Ahn-Crop Crasher is no longer Aryana's. This is exactly the case covered by [Ahn-Crop Crasher ruling #4]: if you gain control of another player's creature until end of turn and exert it, it untaps during that player's untap step.

This outcome is the same whether the game has two players or more than two — the only thing that matters is that control reverts to Noe at end of turn, and Noe's own untap step is unaffected.

question: Andres controls [Strionic Resonator] and plays [Clive's Hideaway]. They activate Strionic Resonator targeting the hideaway trigger, exiling 2 cards. On their next turn, they activate Clive's Hideaway's ability to cast the exiled card. What happens as it resolves?
answer:
Both exiled cards can be played without paying their mana costs (assuming Andres controls four or more legendary creatures when Clive's Hideaway's ability resolves).

Why: Strionic Resonator copies the Hideaway triggered ability of Clive's Hideaway, and a copy of a triggered ability is linked to the same second ability as the original. So when Clive's Hideaway's second ability ({2}, {T}) refers to "the exiled card," it refers to every card exiled by both the original Hideaway trigger and the copy — here, both cards [Strionic Resonator ruling #1]. Rulings on similar linked-ability cases confirm that when the ability gets multiple answers for "the exiled card," it applies to all of them, and you may play none, one, or both [Strionic Resonator ruling #3].

Note also that the copy's source is still Clive's Hideaway [Strionic Resonator ruling #4], and that each Hideaway look/exile happened separately when each instance resolved, since choices made on resolution aren't copied [Strionic Resonator ruling #7].

The "four or more legendary creatures" condition is checked as Clive's Hideaway's {2}, {T} ability resolves; if Andres doesn't control four or more legendary creatures then, he plays nothing and the cards stay exiled. Playing a land among them still uses his land play for the turn, and the cards are played one at a time as the ability resolves.

Nothing here depends on the number of players, so the answer is the same in two-player and multiplayer games.

question: Aminah has no cards in their library and activate [Words of Wind] in their upkeep. Do they lose the game?
answer:
No — activating Words of Wind does not make Aminah lose, and in fact it protects them from the next draw they would make this turn.

Words of Wind reads: "{1}: The next time you would draw a card this turn, each player returns a permanent they control to its owner's hand instead." That's a replacement effect on the draw itself. Merely activating it in the upkeep step doesn't draw anything, so nothing happens involving the empty library at that time; the effect just waits in place.

Then, in Aminah's draw step, the turn-based draw would happen — but Words of Wind replaces it, so no card is ever drawn from the empty library. Instead, each player (Aminah and each opponent) returns a permanent they control to its owner's hand. Because the draw is replaced rather than attempted, Aminah never tries to draw from an empty library and so isn't put in the position that would cost them the game.

Notes and caveats:
- This works for any number of players: the returning effect hits each player who controls a permanent, so at a multiplayer table every player, not just one opponent, returns one.
- If Aminah activates Words of Wind more than once, they can choose which instance to apply and use up each time they would draw a card ([Words of Wind ruling #0]) — one instance per draw, so multiple draws in a turn need multiple activations.
- The protection lasts only for that turn ("this turn"). On a later turn with an empty library and no replacement effect in place, Aminah would have to attempt the draw again.
- The specific numbered rule stating that a player attempting to draw from an empty library loses the game was not included in the context provided to me, so I'm relying on Words of Wind's own text that the draw is replaced and therefore never attempted.

question: Allan controls [Living Inferno]. They activate it, targeting Nathaly's [Runeclaw Bear]. In response, Nathaly casts [Chemister's Trick], targeting the Living Inferno. How much damage will be dealt to Runeclaw Bear when the Living Inferno's ability resolves?
answer:
Runeclaw Bear will be dealt 8 damage — the full amount locked in when Allan activated Living Inferno's ability, unaffected by Chemister's Trick's -2/-0.

Why: because Living Inferno's ability divides damage among targets, the amount of damage it will deal is locked in as the ability is activated, based on Living Inferno's power at that time (8). Later changes to Living Inferno's power — such as the -2/-0 from Nathaly's Chemister's Trick resolving first — don't change that number [Living Inferno ruling #0][Living Inferno ruling #1].

Since Runeclaw Bear was the only target, all 8 damage goes to it, which is lethal to a 2/2. In return, when Living Inferno's ability resolves, Runeclaw Bear deals damage equal to its power to Living Inferno; that amount is determined on resolution, not on activation [Living Inferno ruling #1], so Runeclaw Bear deals 2 damage to Living Inferno. Living Inferno is a 6/5 at that moment due to Chemister's Trick, so 2 damage isn't lethal to it.

Note that Chemister's Trick also makes Living Inferno "attack this turn if able," but Living Inferno was tapped to pay the {T} in its ability's cost, so it won't attack [Chemister's Trick ruling #0]. Nothing here depends on the number of players, so the answer is the same in a two-player or multiplayer game.

Timing assumption: Chemister's Trick was cast in response and so resolves before Living Inferno's ability. If instead the -2/-0 had somehow applied before the ability was activated, Living Inferno would have been a 6/5 at activation and would only have locked in 6 damage.

question: After both players finish taking mulligans, Adrian is going second and has both [Gemstone Caverns] and [Chancellor of the Annex] in their hand. Can they reveal Chancellor of the Annex for its ability and also exile it to begin the game with Gemstone Caverns on the battlefield?
answer:
Yes. Adrian may reveal Chancellor of the Annex from their opening hand and then exile that same Chancellor of the Annex as the cost for putting Gemstone Caverns onto the battlefield.

Why: Both cards grant actions taken from the opening hand (the hand after all mulligans are complete). The starting player takes all of their opening-hand actions first, in any order, then each other player in turn order [Gemstone Caverns ruling #0] [Chancellor of the Annex ruling #2]. Since Adrian is going second, Adrian takes their actions after the starting player, and Adrian chooses the order of their own actions. So Adrian first reveals Chancellor of the Annex, which sets up its effect ("when each opponent casts their first spell of the game, counter that spell unless that player pays {1}"). That revealed effect is established by the act of revealing from the opening hand; it does not require Chancellor of the Annex to stay in hand afterward. Adrian then begins the game with Gemstone Caverns on the battlefield with a luck counter, exiling Chancellor of the Annex as the required "exile a card from your hand."

If Adrian did it in the opposite order — exiling Chancellor of the Annex first — the card would already be in the exile zone and no longer in the opening hand, so it could not then be revealed from hand for its ability. Order matters here, so reveal first.

Multiplayer note: the same works with more than two players; the revealed Chancellor of the Annex effect triggers each time an opponent casts their first spell of the game, i.e., once per opponent [Chancellor of the Annex ruling #1]. In a two-player game it simply applies to the one opponent. Note also the tax is {1} generic mana (payable with any color or colorless), not {C}.

question: Aspen controls [Cosima, God of the Voyage] and mutates [Snapdax, Apex of the Hunt] onto it, putting it underneath Cosima, God of the Voyage. At the beginning of their next upkeep, Aspen exiles Cosima, God of the Voyage to its own triggered ability. What happens?
answer:
Direct answer: Aspen may exile the mutated permanent, and doing so puts both physical cards — Cosima, God of the Voyage and Snapdax, Apex of the Hunt — into exile as two separate cards; the mutated permanent no longer exists. Only Cosima, God of the Voyage carries the granted ability ("Whenever a land you control enters, if Cosima is exiled, you may put a voyage counter on it. If you don't, return Cosima to the battlefield with X +1/+1 counters on it and draw X cards"), so only Cosima, God of the Voyage can come back later, and it comes back as a plain 2/4 Cosima, God of the Voyage — a brand-new object with none of Snapdax, Apex of the Hunt's abilities (no double strike, no mutate trigger). Snapdax, Apex of the Hunt simply stays in exile.

Details and assumptions:
- Cosima, God of the Voyage's ability triggers only if it is on the battlefield at the beginning of Aspen's upkeep, and Aspen may exile it only if it is still on the battlefield as that ability resolves [Cosima, God of the Voyage // The Omenkeel ruling #13]. Here the mutated permanent is Cosima, God of the Voyage (it's the top card), so that works.
- Each land entering under Aspen's control afterward triggers the granted ability; on resolution the game checks that Cosima, God of the Voyage is still in exile, and if it has left exile the ability does nothing [Cosima, God of the Voyage // The Omenkeel ruling #11]. Aspen may choose to return it even with zero voyage counters, drawing no cards and getting no +1/+1 counters [Cosima, God of the Voyage // The Omenkeel ruling #5]. Players cannot respond to the counter-or-return choice [Cosima, God of the Voyage // The Omenkeel ruling #8].
- Because the returned Cosima, God of the Voyage is a new object (a card that left a zone and came back is a new object, per the principle cited in [603.7c]), it is not still mutated and does not gain Snapdax, Apex of the Hunt's abilities. Snapdax, Apex of the Hunt's "Whenever this creature mutates" trigger does not fire again, and nothing returns it.
- Caveat on grounding: the numbered mutate rules were not provided in my context. The closest provided analogue is the merged-permanent rule for meld, [712.21c], which states that when a melded permanent leaves the battlefield one permanent leaves and both cards go to the appropriate zone — the same principle I'm applying to the mutated pile here. If your table wants the literal mutate rule text, look it up; the outcome above matches standard mutate behavior.
- Player count: nothing here depends on the number of opponents, so the answer is the same in a two-player game and at a multiplayer table. (One multiplayer wrinkle from the provided rules: if the controller of a delayed return ability leaves the game, the ability isn't put on the stack and the card never returns [800.4d] — but here Aspen controls both the exile and the return.)

The second ability does not refer to any other object with the same name as the first ability’s source. Gutter Grime has an ability that reads “Whenever a nontoken creature you control dies, put a slime counter on this enchantment, then create a green Ooze creature token with ‘This token’s power and toughness are each equal to the number of slime counters on Gutter Grime.’” The ability granted to the token only looks at the Gutter Grime that created the token, not at any other Gutter Grime on the battlefield. A copy of that token would also have an ability that referred only to the Gutter Grime that created the original token.

Cosima, God of the Voyage and Snapdax, Apex of the Hunt both get exiled and gain the corresponding triggered ability.

question: Aubrey controls [Whiskervale Forerunner] and casts [Growth Cycle] to give it +3/+3. Before it resolves, Aubrey casts [Cooperate] choosing to copy Growth Cycle and changes the target to another creature. Does Whiskervale Forerunner trigger again?
answer:
No. Whiskervale Forerunner does not trigger a second time.

Two independent reasons:

1. The copy of Growth Cycle created by Cooperate doesn't target Whiskervale Forerunner at all — Aubrey changed the copy's target to another creature, which Cooperate expressly permits ("You may choose new targets for the copy") [Refuse // Cooperate ruling #18]. Whiskervale Forerunner's valiant ability only triggers when Whiskervale Forerunner itself becomes the target of a spell or ability Aubrey controls.

2. Even if the copy had kept Whiskervale Forerunner as its target, valiant triggers only "for the first time each turn." Casting Growth Cycle at Whiskervale Forerunner already used up that trigger this turn. A copy on the stack can trigger valiant, but only if the creature hasn't already been targeted by a spell or ability you control this turn [Refuse // Cooperate ruling #1].

Timing/order note: I'm assuming Growth Cycle was cast targeting Whiskervale Forerunner first (triggering valiant then), then Cooperate copied it. The valiant trigger from Growth Cycle resolves before Growth Cycle itself [Whiskervale Forerunner ruling #2], and the Growth Cycle copy resolves before the original Growth Cycle [Refuse // Cooperate ruling #14]. If instead the copy had been the thing that first targeted Whiskervale Forerunner this turn (i.e., original Growth Cycle targeted something else and the copy was pointed at Whiskervale Forerunner), valiant would trigger off the copy [Refuse // Cooperate ruling #1].

Also relevant to the copy's size: Growth Cycle's bonus is locked in as it begins to resolve, and Growth Cycle isn't in the graveyard while it's still on the stack, so it doesn't count itself [Growth Cycle ruling #0][Growth Cycle ruling #1].

None of this depends on player count — the answer is the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).

gold_text.707.10c: To copy a spell, activated ability, or triggered ability means to put a copy of it onto the stack; a copy of a spell isn’t cast and a copy of an activated ability isn’t activated. A copy of a spell or ability copies both the characteristics of the spell or ability and all decisions made for it, including modes, targets, the value of X, and additional or alternative costs. (See rule 601, “Casting Spells.”) Choices that are normally made on resolution are not copied. If an effect of the copy refers to objects used to pay its costs, it uses the objects used to pay the costs of the original spell or ability. A copy of a spell is owned by the player under whose control it was put on the stack. A copy of a spell or ability is controlled by the player under whose control it was put on the stack. A copy of a spell is itself a spell, even though it has no spell card associated with it. A copy of an ability is itself an ability. Some effects copy a spell or ability and state that its controller may choose new targets for the copy. The player may leave any number of the targets unchanged, even if those targets would be illegal. If the player chooses to change some or all of the targets, the new targets must be legal. Once the player has decided what the copy’s targets will be, the copy is put onto the stack with those targets.

answer_gold: No. When copying spells that allow the copies controller to change the target, the targets are changed before the spell is put onto the stack. There is never a point in time where the spell is targeting Whiskervale Forerunner before the targets are changed.

question: Nico has a [Pillarfield Ox] and a [Skullbriar, the Walking Grave] with 3 +1/+1 counters in their graveyard. Arjun casts [Ghastly Conscription], targeting Nico. What happens to the counters on the Skullbriar, the Walking Grave? Will Nico know which manifested card is which?
answer:
The three +1/+1 counters stay with Skullbriar, the Walking Grave, and yes — that will effectively tell everyone which manifested permanent is Skullbriar, the Walking Grave, because it will be a face-down 2/2 with three +1/+1 counters on it (a 5/5), while the manifested Pillarfield Ox will be a plain face-down 2/2.

Why the counters survive: Skullbriar, the Walking Grave's own text says "Counters remain on Skullbriar as it moves to any zone other than a player's hand or library." Ghastly Conscription moves it graveyard → exile → battlefield, and neither of those is a hand or library, so the counters persist through both moves. This card text overrides the general expectation that counters cease to exist when a permanent card changes zones. Per Skullbriar, the Walking Grave ruling #5, it retains all counters, not just +1/+1 counters, and per ruling #2 counters affecting power/toughness apply even in non-battlefield zones (so it's a 4/4 card while in the face-down exile pile).

An important consequence: once it's manifested, the face-down permanent has no name, no mana cost, no creature types, and no abilities (Ghastly Conscription ruling #8) — so it no longer has the counter-retention ability while face down. Compare Skullbriar, the Walking Grave ruling #1: the ability only works if the object has it in the zone it's leaving. So if that face-down permanent later leaves the battlefield while still face down, the counters will cease to exist. Turn it face up (a special action, revealing it and paying {B}{G}, per Ghastly Conscription ruling #2 and #5's framework) and it has the ability again.

Who controls and who knows what: Arjun cast Ghastly Conscription, so Arjun manifests and controls both face-down permanents; Nico only owns the cards. Nico may not look at face-down permanents Nico doesn't control (Ghastly Conscription ruling #13), and the pile is shuffled precisely to hide the identities (ruling #3). But the visible +1/+1 counters defeat that concealment here: the counters are public information on the battlefield, so Nico (and everyone) can identify the counter-laden face-down creature as Skullbriar, the Walking Grave and the other as Pillarfield Ox. Also note Ghastly Conscription ruling #9 — the players must keep clear which face-down permanent is which and how each became face down.

Assumption on timing: I'm treating the counters as already on Skullbriar, the Walking Grave in the graveyard before Ghastly Conscription resolves, as stated. If instead the counters were somehow removed before resolution, the manifested card would just be a face-down 2/2 and would be indistinguishable from the manifested Pillarfield Ox.

Multiplayer: Ghastly Conscription targets a single player, so nothing changes with more than two players — only Nico's graveyard is affected, and Arjun still controls all the manifested permanents; the counters are public info to every player at the table.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).

gold_text.122.2: Counters on an object are not retained if that object moves from one zone to another. The counters are not “removed”; they simply cease to exist. See rule 400.7.
gold_text.406.3: Exiled cards are, by default, kept face up and may be examined by any player at any time. Cards “exiled face down” can’t be examined by any player except when instructions allow it. However, if a player is instructed to look at a card and then exile it face down, or once a player is allowed to look at a card exiled face down, that player may continue to look at that card until it leaves the exile zone or is part of a pile of cards that are shuffled, even if the instruction allowing the player to do so no longer applies.

answer_gold: When in the graveyard, Skullbriar, the Walking Grave had the ability that allowed it to keep its counters, so it is exiled and shuffled with 3 +1/+1 counters. When it's moved to the battlefield, it's face down and no longer has that ability, so the counters cease to exist. It had the counters immediately before entering the battlefield however, so Nico will know which face-down permanent is the Skullbriar, the Walking Grave and which is the Pillarfield Ox.

question: Avery activates [Ascendant Spirit]'s first ability. Before it resolves Avery casts [Slip Out the Back] targeting Ascendant Spirit. When it phases back in, what will it look like?
answer:
Ascendant Spirit phases back in as its normal self — a 1/1 blue Snow Creature — Spirit — with the +1/+1 counter Slip Out the Back put on it, so it's a 2/2 Spirit. It will NOT be a 2/3 Spirit Warrior, because the first ability did nothing.

Why: I'm assuming the ordering you described — the first ability of Ascendant Spirit was activated first, then Slip Out the Back was cast on top of it, so Slip Out the Back resolves first. Slip Out the Back puts a +1/+1 counter on Ascendant Spirit and phases it out. "Phases out" means the permanent (and anything attached to it) is treated as though it doesn't exist until its controller's next turn [Slip Out the Back]. A phased-out permanent can't be affected by spells or abilities and is treated as nonexistent [Slip Out the Back ruling #1], so when the activated ability of Ascendant Spirit then resolves, there is no Ascendant Spirit on the battlefield for it to make into a Spirit Warrior with base power and toughness 2/3; the ability simply does nothing. None of Ascendant Spirit's abilities has a duration, but an ability that never applied leaves nothing behind [Ascendant Spirit ruling #8].

Ascendant Spirit phases in during Avery's untap step, immediately before Avery untaps their permanents, and it keeps the counters it had when it phased out — so the +1/+1 counter is still there, making it 2/2 [Slip Out the Back ruling #2]. Phasing in doesn't trigger enters-the-battlefield abilities [Slip Out the Back ruling #3], and it can attack or pay {T} costs that turn [Slip Out the Back ruling #2]. Avery can, of course, activate the first ability again ({S}{S}) after it phases in to make it a 2/3 Spirit Warrior [Ascendant Spirit ruling #9].

If instead the ability had resolved before Slip Out the Back (i.e., Slip Out the Back was cast after the ability finished resolving), Ascendant Spirit would already be a Spirit Warrior with base power and toughness 2/3, and it would phase back in that way — 3/4 with the +1/+1 counter — since that ability has no duration [Ascendant Spirit ruling #8], [Ascendant Spirit ruling #4].

This interaction doesn't depend on player count; it works the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).

gold_text.702.26e: Phasing If a continuous effect generated by the resolution of a spell or ability modifies the characteristics or changes the controller of any objects, a phased-out permanent won’t be included in the set of affected objects. This includes continuous effects that reference the permanent specifically, unless they also specifically refer to the permanent as phased out.

answer_gold: It will be a 2/2 and not a Warrior. When Ascendant Spirit's ability resolves it's phased out and won't be affected.

question: Aspen controls [Parallel Lives] and a [Caldera Hellion]. They cast [Rite of Replication] targeting the Caldera Hellion. Can Aspen apply the devour replacement effect before the Parallel Lives replacement effect, sacrificing 1 creature to have each token enter with a +1/+1 counter?
answer:
No. Aspen must apply Parallel Lives' replacement effect first, and even then a single sacrificed creature can only give a +1/+1 counter to one of the tokens, not all of them.

Why Parallel Lives goes first: a token entering the battlefield is an event contained within the event of creating that token. When one replacement effect applies to an event and another applies to an event contained within it, the outer one must be chosen first — so the token-doubling of Parallel Lives is applied before any "as this enters" effects such as devour on the resulting tokens [616.1g]. Devour is not an ordering option here at all; it's a replacement effect modifying how each token enters, and it can't be applied to a token that doesn't exist yet.

So, unkicked Rite of Replication creates 1 token, doubled by Parallel Lives to 2 tokens that are copies of Caldera Hellion (kicked, 5 becomes 10) [Parallel Lives ruling #0]. Each token has Devour 1 and each devour works as the token enters [Rite of Replication ruling #11].

Why one sacrifice doesn't feed them all: when multiple permanents with devour are entering at the same time, you may use each one's devour, but the same object can't be chosen to be sacrificed more than once across those replacement effects [614.13b] [Caldera Hellion ruling #3]. Sacrificing 1 creature therefore puts one +1/+1 counter on exactly one token; the others enter with zero counters. Note also that the tokens can't devour each other or themselves [Caldera Hellion ruling #1].

One practical warning: each Caldera Hellion token's triggered ability deals 3 damage to each creature, and tokens that devoured nothing are 3/3s, so that damage will be lethal to them [Caldera Hellion ruling #4].

This analysis doesn't depend on the number of players; Parallel Lives and the devour choices are all made by Aspen as the affected permanents' controller, so it's identical at a two-player or multiplayer table (APNAP ordering in [616.1g] only matters when different players choose simultaneously).

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).

gold_text.616.1g: If two or more replacement and/or prevention effects are attempting to modify the way an event affects an object or player, the affected object’s controller (or its owner if it has no controller) or the affected player chooses one to apply, following the steps listed below. If two or more players have to make these choices at the same time, choices are made in APNAP order (see rule 101.4). While following the steps in 616.1a–f, one replacement or prevention effect may apply to an event, and another may apply to an event contained within the first event. In this case, the second effect can’t be chosen until after the first effect has been chosen. A player is instructed to create a token that’s a copy of Voice of All, which has the ability “As this creature enters, choose a color.” Doubling Season has an ability that reads “If an effect would create one or more tokens under your control, it creates twice that many of those tokens instead.” Because entering the battlefield is an event contained within the event of creating a token, the effect of Doubling Season must be applied first, and then the effects of the two Voice of All tokens may be applied in either order.

One effect reads “If you would gain life, draw that many cards instead,” and another reads “If you would draw a card, return a card from your graveyard to your hand instead.” Both effects combine (regardless of the order they came into existence): Instead of gaining 1 life, the player puts a card from their graveyard into their hand.

Jund (a plane card) says, “Whenever a player casts a black, red, or green creature spell, it gains devour 5.” A player controls Runeclaw Bear and casts Thunder-Thrash Elder, a red creature spell with devour 3. As Thunder-Thrash Elder enters the battlefield, its controller can choose to sacrifice Runeclaw Bear when applying the devour 3 effect or when applying the devour 5 effect, but not both. Thunder-Thrash Elder will enter the battlefield with zero, three, or five +1/+1 counters, depending on this choice.

answer_gold: No. There are two replacement effects trying to apply to the original event of creating a Caldera Hellion: Caldera Hellion's own effect and Parallel Lives's effect. Caldera Hellion's effect applies to it entering the battlefield however, while Parallel Lives's effect applies to it being created, so Parallel Lives's effect must be applied first. After that is applied the original Caldera Hellion's effect doesn't exist anymore, but each of the new Caldera Hellions entering the battlefield has its own effect, which can now be applied individually.

question: Aubrey controls [Exotic Orchard]. Nikolas controls [Crumbling Vestige]. If Aubrey taps Exotic Orchard, what type(s) of mana can it produce?
answer:
Aubrey's Exotic Orchard produces no mana at all in this situation.

Exotic Orchard says "Add one mana of any color that a land an opponent controls could produce," and Exotic Orchard ruling #3 states plainly that the colors of mana are white, blue, black, red, and green, and that Exotic Orchard can't be tapped for colorless mana even if an opponent's land could produce colorless mana. Nikolas's Crumbling Vestige has only one mana ability while it's on the battlefield: "{T}: Add {C}." {C} is colorless mana specifically, not a color and not generic mana, so it gives Exotic Orchard nothing to copy. With no color available, activating Exotic Orchard's ability produces nothing (compare Exotic Orchard ruling #4, where lands with nothing to point at simply produce no mana).

About Crumbling Vestige's other line, "When this land enters, add one mana of any color": that's a one-shot triggered ability that happened as Crumbling Vestige entered the battlefield and is no longer available. It isn't a mana-producing ability Crumbling Vestige has going forward, so it doesn't turn Exotic Orchard on. (If it had still been a standing ability, Exotic Orchard ruling #0's principle of looking only at what the ability produces, not its cost, would matter — but there's no such ability here to check.)

Two-player vs. multiplayer: Exotic Orchard cares about lands *any* opponent controls, so at a larger table Aubrey should check every opponent's lands, not just Nikolas's. If some other opponent controls a land that could produce a color, Exotic Orchard could be tapped for that color. Assuming Aubrey's only opponent is Nikolas, and Crumbling Vestige is his only land, Exotic Orchard makes nothing.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).

gold_text.106.7: Some abilities produce mana based on the type of mana another permanent or permanents “could produce.” The type of mana a permanent could produce at any time includes any type of mana that an ability of that permanent would produce if the ability were to resolve at that time, taking into account any applicable replacement effects in any possible order. Ignore whether any costs of the ability could or could not be paid. If that permanent wouldn’t produce any mana under these conditions, or no type of mana can be defined this way, there’s no type of mana it could produce. Exotic Orchard has the ability “{T}: Add one mana of any color that a land an opponent controls could produce.” If your opponent controls no lands, activating Exotic Orchard’s mana ability will produce no mana. The same is true if you and your opponent each control no lands other than Exotic Orchards. However, if you control a Forest and an Exotic Orchard, and your opponent controls an Exotic Orchard, then each Exotic Orchard could produce {G}.

answer_gold: Any color. Exotic Orchard checks to see what mana Crumbling Vestige could produce if any of its abilities were to resolve at that time. That includes triggered abilities.

question: Azariah, Beckham, and Caelan are playing a multiplayer game. Beckham controls [Stalking Leonin]. Azariah casts [Worst Fears] to take control of Beckham's next turn. After Beckham begins their turn, can Azariah see which player was chosen for the Stalking Leonin?
answer:
Yes — while Azariah controls Beckham's turn, Azariah gets to see Beckham's hidden information, which includes the record of the opponent secretly chosen for Stalking Leonin.

Why: Worst Fears says "You see all cards that player could see and make all decisions for them." While controlling Beckham, Azariah sees all cards in the game that Beckham can see, including Beckham's hand and face-down cards Beckham controls [Worst Fears ruling #11], and Azariah makes all choices and decisions Beckham would make, including whether to activate abilities [Worst Fears ruling #1]. Stalking Leonin's secret choice is recorded and kept with the permanent (for example, a slip of paper with the player's name) [Stalking Leonin ruling #2], and it is information Beckham has; since Azariah must decide whether to pay the "Reveal the player you chose" cost and activate Stalking Leonin's ability, Azariah necessarily has access to that recorded choice.

Important limits:
- Azariah controls only the player, not Beckham's permanents — Stalking Leonin stays under Beckham's control [Worst Fears ruling #4]. So if Azariah activates it during that turn, it can only exile a creature attacking Beckham (the ability's controller), and only if that creature is controlled by the opponent Beckham secretly chose. A creature attacking a planeswalker rather than Beckham can't be targeted [Stalking Leonin ruling #4].
- Azariah must use Beckham's resources to pay Beckham's costs, not their own [Worst Fears ruling #8], and can't make illegal choices [Worst Fears ruling #2].
- The chosen player was locked in when Stalking Leonin entered the battlefield; Azariah can't change it. If Beckham never made a choice (e.g., the permanent became a copy of Stalking Leonin), the cost can't be paid at all [Stalking Leonin ruling #0].

Multiplayer note: this is inherently a multiplayer situation (Stalking Leonin requires choosing an opponent, and here there are three players — Azariah, Beckham, and Caelan). Nothing changes about the visibility answer based on player count; the secret choice could be Azariah or Caelan, and Azariah learning it is exactly one of the effects of controlling Beckham.

Timing assumption: I'm assuming Worst Fears already resolved and Beckham's controlled turn has begun, as stated. Before that turn begins, Azariah has no access to the information.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).

gold_text.722.4: In every zone, a preparation card has only its normal characteristics.

answer_gold: No. The choice was made as Stalking Leonin entered the battlefield, which already happened- it's no longer visible to Beckham. Azariah can choose to activate the ability (at which point all players will know who was chosen), but otherwise the choice is not visible to any player.

question: Angela controls [Mirror Gallery] and two [Sakashima the Impostor]s. One is a copy of their [Master of the Hunt]; the other is copying a wolf token created by Master of the Hunt. They attack with all four creatures. What are the possible bands that Angela may declare?
answer:
Angela can't declare any bands — all four creatures must attack individually.

The only banding ability in play is the one granted by Master of the Hunt to its tokens: "bands with other creatures named Wolves of the Hunt." As the reminder text on Master of the Hunt spells out, "Any creatures named Wolves of the Hunt can attack in a band as long as at least one has 'bands with other creatures named Wolves of the Hunt.'" That restricts the band to creatures actually named Wolves of the Hunt, and a band needs at least two creatures.

Look at the four attackers:
- Master of the Hunt itself — named Master of the Hunt, has no banding ability, so it can't join.
- The Wolves of the Hunt token — has the banding ability, but it's the only creature with that name on the battlefield.
- The Sakashima the Impostor copying Master of the Hunt — Sakashima the Impostor's own text says the copy's name is Sakashima the Impostor, so it isn't named Wolves of the Hunt (and Master of the Hunt has no banding ability anyway).
- The Sakashima the Impostor copying the Wolves of the Hunt token — it does copy the ability "bands with other creatures named Wolves of the Hunt," but again its name is Sakashima the Impostor, not Wolves of the Hunt, so it isn't a legal member of that band either.

So there's exactly one creature named Wolves of the Hunt, and a one-creature "band" is just a normal attacker. Mirror Gallery is doing real work here (it lets the two legendary Sakashima the Impostors coexist, per Mirror Gallery ruling #0), but it doesn't change any names, so it doesn't enable a band.

If Angela activates Master of the Hunt (or the Sakashima the Impostor that copies Master of the Hunt) before attackers are declared to make a second Wolves of the Hunt token, those two tokens could then attack as a band.

Note: the numbered banding rules weren't provided in my context, so this answer rests on the reminder text printed on Master of the Hunt and on Sakashima the Impostor's name-changing clause; the general banding rules could add further restrictions on band size or composition. Nothing here depends on the number of opponents, though with more than two players every creature in a band would have to be attacking the same defending player or their planeswalker/battle.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).

gold_text.702.22c: Banding As a player declares attackers, they may declare that one or more attacking creatures with banding and up to one attacking creature without banding (even if it has “bands with other”) are all in a “band.” They may also declare that one or more attacking [quality] creatures with “bands with other [quality]” and any number of other attacking [quality] creatures are all in a band. A player may declare as many attacking bands as they want, but each creature may be a member of only one of them. (Defending players can’t declare bands but may use banding in a different way; see rule 702.22j.)

answer_gold: No bands can be declared. The only creature on the battlefield named "Wolves of the Hunt" is the token, so it cannot declare itself as in a band with anything else. The Sakashima the Impostor with "bands with other creatures named Wolves of the Hunt" is not itself named "Wolves of the Hunt", so it cannot declare itself as in a band with the token.

question: Avery controls a Germ token that's equipped with [Barbed Bloodletter]. Nadia controls two [Teferi's Curse]s, one on the Germ, the other on the Barbed Bloodletter. During Avery's untap step, which permanents will phase out? Which of these will phase back in?
answer:
Both permanents that Nadia has enchanted — Avery's Germ token and the Barbed Bloodletter equipping it — phase out during Avery's untap step, and both are set to phase back in at the start of Avery's next untap step (before Avery untaps).

Why: "Phasing" means a permanent alternately phases out and phases in; while phased out it's treated as though it doesn't exist. Teferi's Curse grants "Enchanted permanent has phasing," and its reminder text specifies the timing: "It phases in or out before its controller untaps during each of their untap steps." Note that the relevant controller is the controller of the permanent that has phasing (Avery), not Nadia who controls the Auras. So:
- Germ token: has phasing from one Teferi's Curse, is controlled by Avery, so it phases out in Avery's untap step and would phase in during Avery's following untap step.
- Barbed Bloodletter: has phasing from the other Teferi's Curse, is also controlled by Avery, so it likewise phases out now and would phase in during Avery's following untap step.

Two things the provided context does not settle, so I won't guess at them: (1) whether the two Teferi's Curses themselves phase out along with the permanents they enchant (the general phasing rules about attached permanents phasing indirectly weren't provided), and (2) whether a phased-out token like the Germ still exists to phase back in. Those depend on the full phasing rules (and token-existence rules), which aren't in the context here.

Nothing in this interaction depends on the number of players, so the answer is the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table.

question: Alessandra controls [Sheoldred, the Apocalypse]. During their main phase, they cast [Day's Undoing]. How much life does each player gain/lose?
answer:
No life is gained or lost at all.

Day's Undoing makes each player shuffle hand and graveyard into their library and draw seven cards, and Sheoldred, the Apocalypse does trigger — seven times for Alessandra's own draws ("you gain 2 life") and seven times for each opponent's draws ("they lose 2 life"). But because Alessandra cast Day's Undoing on their own turn, Day's Undoing then ends the turn. Per [Day's Undoing ruling #5], any abilities that trigger while players are shuffling cards into their library or drawing seven cards cease to exist when the turn ends — they are never put onto the stack. So all fourteen-plus Sheoldred, the Apocalypse triggers simply vanish and nothing resolves.

Supporting detail: ending the turn exiles everything on the stack, and during that process no player gets priority and no triggered abilities are put onto the stack ([Day's Undoing ruling #4]). The only triggers that could still matter are ones put onto the stack during the cleanup step ([Day's Undoing ruling #2]), which is not the case for these draw triggers.

Two players vs. multiplayer: the result is the same. With more opponents there are simply more Sheoldred, the Apocalypse triggers for the extra players' draws, and all of them equally cease to exist, so no player at the table loses or gains life.

Timing caveat: this assumes Day's Undoing resolved on Alessandra's own turn, as stated. If Day's Undoing had somehow resolved during another player's turn, the turn would not end, and then all the Sheoldred, the Apocalypse triggers would resolve normally — Alessandra would gain 14 life, and each opponent would lose 14 life (with Alessandra choosing the order of simultaneous-draw triggers, per [Sheoldred, the Apocalypse ruling #0]).

Multiple player-controlling effects that affect the same player overwrite each other. The last one to be created is the one that works.

answer_gold: None. The players first draw seven cards each, triggering Sheoldred, the Apocalypse fourteen times. Then Alessandra ends the turn, which nullifies those triggers before they're even put onto the stack.

question: It is currently day and Adonis controls [Lazotep Convert] (the back face of [Invasion of Amonkhet]), which is a copy of [Kessig Naturalist]. What happens if it becomes night?
answer:
Nothing changes about Adonis's permanent: Lazotep Convert copying Kessig Naturalist does not transform when it becomes night. It stays on the battlefield as a 2/2 Human Werewolf named Kessig Naturalist (a 4/4 black Zombie in addition to its other colors and types, per Lazotep Convert's own text), keeping daybound.

Why: Lazotep Convert's copy effect copies exactly what was printed on the copied creature card [Invasion of Amonkhet // Lazotep Convert ruling #12], so it gains Kessig Naturalist's printed text, including daybound. Normally daybound permanents transform to their nightbound faces as it becomes night, immediately and not as a state-based action [Kessig Naturalist // Lord of the Ulvenwald ruling #2]. But the physical card here is Invasion of Amonkhet // Lazotep Convert, already on its Lazotep Convert (back) face; the copy effect only gives it the copiable characteristics of the Kessig Naturalist face, not Lord of the Ulvenwald as a second face to turn to. With no Lord of the Ulvenwald face available to it, the daybound transform simply can't happen and the permanent is unaffected. Note also that permanents with daybound/nightbound can't transform by any other means [Kessig Naturalist // Lord of the Ulvenwald ruling #8], so no other effect will flip it back to Invasion of Amonkhet either.

Timing note: I'm assuming Lazotep Convert was already on the battlefield as a copy of Kessig Naturalist before night fell. If instead it were entering the battlefield while it is already night, the daybound rule about entering with the nightbound face up [Kessig Naturalist // Lord of the Ulvenwald ruling #6] still couldn't apply, for the same reason — there is no Lord of the Ulvenwald face for it, so it just enters as the Kessig Naturalist copy.

Caveat: the provided context doesn't include the general copy rules (what a copy of a double-faced card copies), so that step of the reasoning rests on Lazotep Convert ruling #12 rather than a quoted numbered rule. Day/night is a game-wide designation, so this works the same in two-player and multiplayer games [Kessig Naturalist // Lord of the Ulvenwald ruling #4].

question: Adelina's [Fireblade Charger] dies, and Nasir responds with [Thwart the Enemy]. Is the damage prevented?
answer:
No — Thwart the Enemy does not prevent Fireblade Charger's death-trigger damage.

Why: Thwart the Enemy only prevents damage "that would be dealt this turn by creatures your opponents control." Once Fireblade Charger has died, it is a card in Adelina's graveyard, not a creature Adelina controls on the battlefield, so the damage source isn't among the objects Thwart the Enemy covers. Fireblade Charger's triggered ability ("When this creature dies, it deals damage equal to its power to any target") still resolves, using Fireblade Charger's last known existence on the battlefield to determine its power — if that power was 0 or less, the ability simply does nothing [Fireblade Charger ruling #0].

Timing assumption: I'm assuming Nasir cast Thwart the Enemy in response to the death trigger (i.e., after Fireblade Charger had already left the battlefield). That's the only order the question describes. If instead Thwart the Enemy had resolved earlier in the turn while Fireblade Charger was still on the battlefield, the answer would be the same for the death trigger, because at the time that damage is actually dealt Fireblade Charger is no longer a creature an opponent controls — the prevention effect's description of the source is checked when the damage would be dealt.

Multiplayer note: nothing here changes with more than two players. Thwart the Enemy says "creatures your opponents control," so it would cover on-battlefield creatures of every opponent, not just Adelina's — but Fireblade Charger in the graveyard is still not covered.

Practical upshot: Nasir needs a way to prevent or redirect damage from a non-creature/graveyard source, or to reduce Fireblade Charger's power before it dies, rather than Thwart the Enemy.

answer_gold: Unclear. Fireblade Charger is not currently a creature on the battlefield, but the game uses its last known information to determine how the damage is dealt. If Fireblade Charger only applies to objects that are creatures, like how Biomantic Mastery only counts creatures that actually exist on the battlefield, it won't be prevented. But if Fireblade Charger checks the source of damage to see whether it's a creature, it will be able to identify the damage as coming from a creature. The intention is probably the latter, but Wizards has not clarified.

question: Nico controls Analia's [Bane Alley Blackguard] enchanted with their [Corrupted Conscience]. Analia casts their own [Lay Claim], targeting Nico's Corrupted Conscience. After it resolves, who controls the Bane Alley Blackguard? Who controls the Corrupted Conscience?
answer:
Analia ends up controlling both. Lay Claim enchants Nico's Corrupted Conscience and says "You control enchanted permanent," so Analia becomes the controller of Corrupted Conscience. Corrupted Conscience in turn says "You control enchanted creature," and that "you" refers to whoever currently controls Corrupted Conscience — now Analia — so control of Bane Alley Blackguard passes to Analia as well.

The Lay Claim ruling makes the key point explicit: an Aura's effect that refers to "you" applies to that Aura's controller, not to some earlier controller. Gaining control of a permanent doesn't by itself move Auras attached to it, but here Lay Claim is attached directly to Corrupted Conscience, and Corrupted Conscience remains attached to Bane Alley Blackguard. Corrupted Conscience's control-changing effect is continuous and simply starts pointing at its new controller, so no new trigger or re-targeting is needed.

Side effects: Bane Alley Blackguard still has infect from Corrupted Conscience, and since Analia owns Bane Alley Blackguard, she now controls a creature she owns again. If Analia later loses control of Corrupted Conscience (Lay Claim leaves the battlefield, for example), control of Corrupted Conscience reverts to Nico, and with it control of Bane Alley Blackguard.

This result doesn't depend on the number of players — it works identically in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table, since only the Aura controllers matter.

question: Autumn controls [Traveling Chocobo] and casts [Phyrexian Ingester]. Autumn exiles [Scarwood Goblins] and then [Tor Giant] with the triggers. What are Phyrexian Ingester's power and toughness?
answer:
Phyrexian Ingester ends up 5/5 — and only one card gets exiled, not two. Traveling Chocobo's last ability only applies when "a land or Bird you control" enters the battlefield. Phyrexian Ingester is a Creature — Phyrexian Beast, not a land and not a Bird, so its Imprint trigger ("When this creature enters, you may exile target nontoken creature") triggers only once. Autumn exiles just one creature; with Scarwood Goblins (2/2) exiled, Phyrexian Ingester gets +2/+2 and is 5/5, and if instead Tor Giant (3/3) were the one exiled it would be +3/+3 for a 6/6. Tor Giant and Scarwood Goblins can't both be exiled off this cast.

For completeness: had the entering permanent actually been a land or Bird Autumn controlled, the ability would trigger an additional time, each instance choosing its own target separately (Traveling Chocobo ruling #11), and when a linked ability asks about "the exiled card" and gets multiple answers used for a variable, the sum is used (Traveling Chocobo ruling #8) — that would have given +5/+5 from Scarwood Goblins plus Tor Giant, an 8/8. Note also that the bonus uses the cards' power and toughness as they exist in exile, ignoring counters, Auras, and Equipment they had on the battlefield (Phyrexian Ingester rulings #1 and #2), and it updates continuously if those values change.

Nothing here depends on the number of players; the answer is the same in a two-player or multiplayer game, except that in a Two-Headed Giant game Traveling Chocobo's ability wouldn't affect triggered abilities of permanents Autumn's teammate controls (Traveling Chocobo ruling #6).

If that ability asks for any information about the exiled card, such as a characteristic or mana value, it gets multiple answers. If these answers are used to determine the value of a variable, the sum of the answers is used. If that ability performs any actions on “the” card, it performs that action on each exiled card. If that ability creates a token that is a copy of “the” card, then for each exiled card, it creates a token that is a copy of that card. If that ability performs any actions on “a” card, the controller of the ability chooses which card is affected.

answer_gold:
It's an 8/8.

The enter-the-battlefield ability of Phyrexian Ingester is part of a pair of linked abilities. When determining a value for Phyrexian Ingester's second ability, the sum of the powers and toughnesses from Scarwood Goblins and Tor Giant is used. This gives Phyrexian Ingester +5/+5, which makes it an 8/8.

question: Beverly controls [Pandemonium]. Adalynn casts [Knight Errant] and targets Beverly's [Forest Bear] with the Pandemonium trigger. In response Channing casts [Ral's Outburst] targeting Adalynn causing them to lose the game. Will Beverly's creature die?
answer:
Yes — Beverly's Forest Bear is dealt 2 damage and dies (assuming the choices were already made, as the question states, and Ral's Outburst resolves before the Pandemonium trigger).

Why: Beverly controls Pandemonium, so Beverly controls the triggered ability even though Adalynn, as the controller of the entering Knight Errant, is the one who chooses the target and chooses whether to have it deal damage [Pandemonium ruling #1]. Because Beverly controls the ability, Adalynn losing the game doesn't remove that ability from the stack.

Adalynn's Knight Errant leaves the battlefield when Adalynn leaves the game, but Pandemonium's ability doesn't check the creature's power until it resolves, and if the creature is no longer on the battlefield it deals damage equal to its power immediately before it left [Pandemonium ruling #0]. Knight Errant is a 2/2, so Forest Bear (a 2/2) takes 2 damage and is destroyed.

Timing note: I'm assuming Adalynn already declared the target (Forest Bear) and chose to have Knight Errant deal damage before Channing cast Ral's Outburst, since Ral's Outburst was cast "in response" to the trigger. If instead Adalynn were gone before those choices existed (i.e., the trigger hadn't been put on the stack with a target yet), there'd be no target/choice and Forest Bear would survive.

This is inherently a multiplayer situation (three players). The provided rules context doesn't include the rules governing exactly what happens when a player leaves the game mid-resolution — objects they control leaving, choices they were to make, etc. — so that portion rests on the Pandemonium rulings above rather than on a numbered rule I was given.

question: Asher casts [Show and Tell]. As it resolves, Asher wants to put [Hall of Triumph] onto the battlefield. Do they know what Noa is putting onto the battlefield while making the choice for Hall of Triumph's replacement effect?
answer:
No — Asher must choose Hall of Triumph's color before Noa's card is revealed, so Asher generally does not know what Noa is putting onto the battlefield.

Here's the sequence during Show and Tell's resolution. First, every player chooses their card: the active player (Asher) chooses first, then each other player in turn order, and a player need not reveal the chosen card so long as it's clear which physical card was chosen [Show and Tell ruling #2]. Only after all players have chosen are choices required by the cards themselves made — again active player first, then the others in turn order [Show and Tell ruling #0]. Hall of Triumph's "As Hall of Triumph enters, choose a color" is exactly such a choice, so Asher names the color at that point, before any card actually hits the battlefield.

Because the cards are only put onto the battlefield simultaneously after all those choices are made [Show and Tell ruling #2], Noa's card is still just an unrevealed (but identified) card in hand when Asher names the color. Asher knows a card was chosen and which one it is physically, but not its identity unless Noa voluntarily revealed it or prior information gave it away.

Note also that "as ... enters" choices of this kind are made as part of the permanent entering, not as a separate later action [613.2a].

Multiplayer note: with more than two players, the same order applies — Asher (active player) chooses the color first, then each other player in turn order makes their card's choices, so Asher is the least informed of all. In a strict two-player game it's just Asher then Noa. Asher never gets to wait and see.

question: Adriel controls [Wandering Ones] equipped with [Fleetfeather Sandals]. On Nico's turn, they enchant it with [Tightening Coils]. On Adriel's next turn, they activate Fleetfeather Sandals's equip ability, targeting Wandering Ones. After that resolves, does it have flying?
answer:
The provided rules don't settle this one. The answer turns entirely on timestamp order under rule 613.7 (and specifically on whether re-attaching an Equipment to the same creature it's already attached to gives its granted-ability effect a new timestamp), and rule 613.7 is not included in the context I was given.

What the context does establish:
- Fleetfeather Sandals grants "Equipped creature has flying and haste," and Tightening Coils says "Enchanted creature gets -6/-0 and loses flying." Both are continuous effects modifying Wandering Ones' abilities, so which one applies last decides whether Wandering Ones has flying.
- [Tightening Coils ruling #0] states that if an effect gives the enchanted creature flying after Tightening Coils became attached to it, the creature will have flying. So if activating Fleetfeather Sandals's equip ability counts as giving Wandering Ones flying anew (a fresh timestamp), Wandering Ones would have flying; if the equip does not refresh the timestamp because Fleetfeather Sandals was already attached to Wandering Ones, Tightening Coils remains later and Wandering Ones would not have flying.

To resolve it I would need rule 613.7 (timestamps, including the rule on when an Aura's or Equipment's timestamp changes upon becoming attached to a different object). Note also that Tightening Coils' -6/-0 applies in layer 7 (rule 613.1g) regardless, so Wandering Ones is a -5/1 either way. This analysis doesn't depend on player count, so it's the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table.
