question: Addilynn activates the Unearth ability of their [Extractor Demon], returning it to the battlefield. Before their end step, Addilynn casts [Reality Ripple] targeting Extractor Demon. What happens to it?
answer:
Short answer: the provided rules don't settle this, so I can't give you a confident resolution. Here's what the given card text does establish and what's missing.

What we know from the cards themselves: Reality Ripple makes target artifact, creature, or land phase out, and its reminder text tells us that while a permanent is phased out "it's treated as though it doesn't exist" and "it phases in before its controller untaps during their next untap step." Extractor Demon's Unearth ability says the card is returned from the graveyard, gains haste, and is exiled "at the beginning of the next end step or if it would leave the battlefield."

So the interaction hinges on two things: (1) whether phasing out counts as Extractor Demon "leaving the battlefield" (which would trigger Unearth's exile replacement/trigger), and (2) whether Unearth's delayed exile at the beginning of the next end step still applies to a permanent that is phased out and therefore "treated as though it doesn't exist." The rules excerpts I was given cover only counters, layers/timestamps, and state-based actions about counters — there are no phasing rules (nothing on rule 702.26 or on which zone a phased-out permanent occupies), and no rules on leaves-the-battlefield events or delayed triggered abilities. Without those, I'd be guessing.

Also note this answer would be identical in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table; nothing here depends on the number of players, and no multiplayer rule was provided.

To resolve it, you'd need the phasing rules (in particular whether a phased-out permanent remains on the battlefield and whether phasing out is a zone change) plus the delayed-trigger rules for Unearth.

answer_gold: Extractor Demon phases out. When the unearth trigger resolves during Addilynn's end step, it won't be exiled. It will phase back in during Addilynn's next untap step, after which point it will be exiled instead of being put anywhere else if it would leave the battlefield.

question: Avery controls [Vhal, Candlekeep Researcher] and Natalie controls [Verity Circle] and [Koskun Falls]. Avery attacks Natalie with Vhal, Candlekeep Researcher, and then taps it to pay for the cost required by Koskun Falls. Will Natalie's Verity Circle trigger?
answer:
Yes — Natalie's Verity Circle triggers, and Natalie may draw a card.

Why: Vhal, Candlekeep Researcher has vigilance, so it doesn't become tapped when it's declared as an attacker; it's still untapped after attackers are declared. Koskun Falls' attack restriction demands {2} generic mana for each creature attacking Natalie, and Avery pays it by activating Vhal, Candlekeep Researcher's ability ({T}: add {C} equal to its toughness, here 3 colorless). That activation actually changes Vhal, Candlekeep Researcher from untapped to tapped, which is what Verity Circle looks for [Verity Circle ruling #1]. The tap happens after the declare attackers step's declaration, not as part of declaring it as an attacker, so the "if it isn't being declared as an attacker" condition is satisfied — exactly the vigilance case spelled out in [Verity Circle ruling #2].

Notes: the {C} produced can't be spent to cast spells from Avery's hand, but paying the {2} generic cost imposed by Koskun Falls isn't casting a spell, so colorless mana works there ({2} generic is payable with colorless). Also, Koskun Falls' upkeep trigger (tap an untapped creature you control) is Natalie's own obligation and involves Natalie's creatures, not Vhal, Candlekeep Researcher — the cost Avery pays is the {2}-per-attacker mana cost.

This works the same in a two-player game and at a multiplayer table; Koskun Falls only taxes creatures attacking Natalie, and Verity Circle triggers off any creature an opponent of Natalie controls becoming tapped.

Therefore, tapping Vhal, Candlekeep Researcher to pay for the cost required by Koskun Falls is part of declaring it as an attacker.

question: Nico controls [Platinum Emperion]. Alexandra attacks with [Hopeful Eidolon], which Nico doesn't block. Does Alexandra gain life?
answer:
Yes — Alexandra gains 1 life. Hopeful Eidolon deals 1 damage to Nico; because of Platinum Emperion, Nico's life total doesn't change (no life lost), but Platinum Emperion only affects its controller's life total, not Alexandra's. Hopeful Eidolon's lifelink still causes its controller, Alexandra, to gain that much life.

This is exactly the case covered by [Platinum Emperion ruling #3]: Platinum Emperion doesn't prevent damage, it only changes the result of that damage for Nico — "if a creature with lifelink deals damage to you, you won't lose any life, but its controller will still gain that much life." Damage is still dealt, so damage-triggered abilities would also still trigger ([Platinum Emperion ruling #4]).

This holds the same whether the game has two players or more; Platinum Emperion's text ("Your life total can't change") applies only to Nico, so any other player damaged by a lifelink source loses life normally and Alexandra's life gain is unaffected.

Yes. Damage can have 0 or more results. Normally a creature with lifelink dealing damage to a player would have two results:

* Its controller gains that much life.
* The recipient of the damage loses that much life.

Platinum Emperion makes the second result impossible, so only the first occurs.

question: Ari casts a [Hero of Oxid Ridge]. In response, Nixon casts [Hallow], targeting the Hero of Oxid Ridge. When Ari attacks with the Hero of Oxid Ridge that turn, will the damage be prevented?
answer:
No — the Hero of Oxid Ridge will deal its combat damage normally.

Hallow says "Prevent all damage target spell would deal this turn." That shield is attached to the object Hallow targeted: the Hero of Oxid Ridge *spell* on the stack. A creature spell like Hero of Oxid Ridge doesn't deal any damage while it's a spell, so the prevention effect simply never has anything to prevent. When the Hero of Oxid Ridge spell resolves it becomes a permanent — a creature with the card type Creature and the subtypes Human and Knight ([Creature], [302.3], [205.3b]) — and combat damage in the combat damage step is dealt by that creature permanent, not by the spell Hallow targeted. Nothing in Hallow's text extends the prevention to the resulting permanent, so Nixon has effectively wasted the Hallow (a common use for Hallow is targeting a damage-dealing spell such as a burn spell, where it prevents the damage and gains that much life).

Assumption on timing: I'm reading this as Hallow being cast while the Hero of Oxid Ridge is still on the stack (which is the only way Hallow can legally target it, since Hallow targets a spell). If instead the Hero of Oxid Ridge had already resolved, Hallow couldn't target it at all and the cast would be illegal.

Also note what does still apply: Hero of Oxid Ridge has haste, so it can attack the turn it resolves, and its attack triggers give each other attacking creature +1/+0 and stop creatures with power 1 or less from blocking — power being checked when blockers are declared ([Hero of Oxid Ridge ruling #0], [Hero of Oxid Ridge ruling #1]).

This answer doesn't depend on player count: it's the same in a two-player game and at a multiplayer table, except that in multiplayer Ari chooses which opponent (or which planeswalker/battle) the Hero of Oxid Ridge attacks.

question: Ariel controls [Mycosynth Lattice]. Nora controls [Kaslem's Strider] enchanted with [Spirit Away]. Ariel casts [Opportunistic Dragon] and takes control of Spirit Away. What will happen after Opportunistic Dragon's ability resolves?
answer:
Ariel ends up controlling Spirit Away, but Spirit Away loses all abilities — including "You control enchanted creature," "+2/+2" and "flying" — so control of Kaslem's Strider goes back to its owner/normal controller Nora, and Kaslem's Strider is just a 5/5 artifact creature Golem with no flying.

Why: Mycosynth Lattice says "All permanents are artifacts in addition to their other types," and that includes Auras on the battlefield (see Mycosynth Lattice ruling #3, which confirms Auras become artifacts). So Spirit Away is an artifact permanent Nora controls and is a legal choice for Opportunistic Dragon's "choose target Human or artifact an opponent controls." (Mycosynth Lattice ruling #1 notes only battlefield permanents are affected, which Spirit Away is.)

When the ability resolves, Ariel gains control of Spirit Away and Spirit Away "loses all abilities." Its control-changing ability is what was letting Nora control Kaslem's Strider; with that ability gone, Kaslem's Strider reverts to Nora, and it no longer gets +2/+2 or flying. Spirit Away remains attached to Kaslem's Strider (it isn't unattached — Mycosynth Lattice alone doesn't make it a creature; only with something like March of the Machines would it become a creature and fall off per Mycosynth Lattice ruling #3). Spirit Away also "can't attack or block," which is irrelevant while it isn't a creature.

This lasts for as long as Opportunistic Dragon remains on the battlefield; if Opportunistic Dragon leaves later, Nora gets Spirit Away back and it regains its abilities, so she'd again control Kaslem's Strider. Note Opportunistic Dragon ruling #1: the effect doesn't expire just because someone else gains control of Opportunistic Dragon, and per Opportunistic Dragon ruling #0, even if a third player gains control of Spirit Away it still has no abilities.

Timing assumption: I'm assuming Mycosynth Lattice was already on the battlefield when Opportunistic Dragon's triggered ability was put on the stack and chose its target, which is required for Spirit Away to be a legal artifact target. If Mycosynth Lattice left the battlefield before the ability resolved, Spirit Away would no longer be an artifact, the target would be illegal, and the ability would do nothing. Also, per Opportunistic Dragon ruling #3, if Opportunistic Dragon itself left the battlefield before the ability resolved, Ariel gains control of nothing at all.

Player count doesn't change any of this — Opportunistic Dragon simply requires the chosen permanent to be one an opponent controls, so with more than two players Ariel may pick any opponent's Human or artifact.

answer_gold: Spirit Away will continue to be attached to Kaslem's Strider indefinitely. The "enchant" keyword is a restriction on what an Aura can enchant- without it Spirit Away is legally able to enchant anything.

question: Atlas attacks with [Pristine Angel], and Nico targets it with [Cephalid Snitch] before blockers. After combat, Atlas casts a spell, untapping Pristine Angel. Once untapped, can Nico target it with [Mob]?
answer:
Yes — Nico can cast Mob targeting Pristine Angel.

Why: Cephalid Snitch's ability says "Target creature loses protection from black until end of turn." That is a continuous effect lasting the whole turn, and it applies on top of Pristine Angel's own static ability ("As long as this creature is untapped, it has protection from artifacts and from each color") because Cephalid Snitch's effect has the later timestamp — a later effect that removes an ability is applied after the earlier ability that grants it (613.7c describes this timestamp ordering principle). So even after Atlas's spell untaps Pristine Angel via "Whenever you cast a spell, you may untap this creature," Pristine Angel regains protection from artifacts and from white, blue, red, and green, but not from black, for the rest of that turn. Mob is a black instant, so it can legally target Pristine Angel and destroy it.

Timing assumption: Nico sacrificed Cephalid Snitch this same turn ("before blockers"), and Atlas's spell resolves later in that same turn, so "until end of turn" is still in effect. Note that it doesn't matter that Pristine Angel was tapped when Cephalid Snitch resolved — Cephalid Snitch's ability doesn't require the target to actually have protection from black, and the effect keeps working for the turn. If instead the untap happened on a later turn, the Cephalid Snitch effect would have expired and untapped Pristine Angel would have protection from black, making it an illegal target for Mob.

One caution: Pristine Angel's protection from artifacts and from each other color is fully back once it's untapped, so only black spells and abilities (and non-artifact, non-colored sources) can affect it.

This analysis is the same whether it's a two-player game or a multiplayer table; nothing here depends on the number of players.

answer_gold: Yes. "Protection from all colors" means the same thing as an individual protection ability for each color, so Pristine Angel will lose protection from black while still having protection from all other colors and from artifacts.

question: Ashley controls a [Gaea's Liege] and 1 [Bayou]. Naomi controls a [Reverence] and 3 Bayous. Can Ashley attack with the Gaea's Liege?
answer:
No — Gaea's Liege can't be declared as an attacker against Naomi. 

Why: while Gaea's Liege isn't attacking, its power and toughness each equal the number of Forests Ashley controls. Ashley's single Bayou has the basic land types Swamp and Forest, so it counts as a Forest [Bayou ruling #0], making Gaea's Liege a 1/1 at that moment. The check for legality of attacking happens as attackers are declared, and Gaea's Liege's own ruling says you use the "not attacking" power and toughness at declaration — the attacking-based value (Forests the defending player controls, here 3) only applies after declaration is complete [Gaea's Liege ruling #0]. Since Gaea's Liege has power 1 (2 or less) at declaration, Reverence's "Creatures with power 2 or less can't attack you" forbids the attack, and a "can't" effect beats permission [101.2].

Two ways Ashley could still get an attack in:
- Attack a planeswalker Naomi controls instead: Reverence only stops attacks on Naomi herself, not on her planeswalkers [Reverence ruling #0].
- Raise Gaea's Liege's power before declaration by making more of Ashley's lands Forests. Gaea's Liege's own {T} ability ("Target land becomes a Forest") requires tapping Gaea's Liege, and a tapped creature can't be declared as an attacker, so that particular ability doesn't help on the same turn; another Forest-making or land-dropping effect would.

Multiplayer note: if this is a two-player game, Gaea's Liege simply can't attack (except a planeswalker). At a table with more than two players, Reverence only protects Naomi, so Ashley could declare Gaea's Liege as an attacker against a different opponent; its power would then be based on that defending player's Forests once declaration is complete.

question: Arjun's [Morality Shift] resolves, in what order do they put cards in their graveyard?
answer:
Arjun chooses the order. When Morality Shift resolves and exchanges Arjun's graveyard and library, Arjun may choose the order in which the cards that were in his library are placed into his graveyard ([Morality Shift ruling #0]). The cards going the other way (former graveyard cards becoming his library) are then shuffled, as Morality Shift instructs, so their order doesn't matter.

Note also that Morality Shift works even if Arjun's graveyard or library is empty ([Morality Shift ruling #1]). Nothing here depends on the number of players, so the answer is the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table.

question: Ares controls [Gaea's Cradle] and no creatures. Nico controls a [Contamination]. If Ares taps the Gaea's Cradle, what mana is produced, if any?
answer:
Tapping Gaea's Cradle produces one {B}. Contamination's second ability reads "If a land is tapped for mana, it produces {B} instead of any other type and amount," and that text replaces both the color and the quantity of mana the land would have made. So even though Gaea's Cradle would normally produce {G} for each creature Ares controls — zero mana with no creatures — the replacement effect from Nico's Contamination substitutes a single {B}.

Why the card text controls: Contamination's second ability is a replacement effect, not a triggered ability [Contamination ruling #0], so it applies at the moment Gaea's Cradle is tapped for mana, before any mana is actually added to Ares's mana pool. Because the printed text explicitly overrides "any other type and amount," it beats the land's own amount-setting text. The exception in [Contamination ruling #2] is only about *external* effects (things like mana doublers) — those still add their extra mana as directed, and effects that scale off the type produced are changed in color but not in amount. Gaea's Cradle's own "for each creature you control" is not an external effect, so it is fully replaced.

Assumption on timing: I'm reading this as Contamination already on the battlefield and resolved when Gaea's Cradle is tapped. If Gaea's Cradle were tapped for mana first and Contamination entered afterward, the replacement effect would have nothing to apply to and Ares would simply have gotten no mana.

Multiplayer note: Contamination says "a land," not "a land you control," so it affects every player's lands identically. The answer is the same at a two-player table or with more than two players; nothing here depends on player count. The provided context contains no multiplayer-specific rule that would change this.

See rule 605, “Mana Abilities.” A replacement effect that applies if a permanent “is tapped for mana” or tapped for mana of a specific type and/or amount modifies the mana production event while such an ability is resolving and producing mana or the specified type and/or amount of mana.

answer_gold: No mana is produced. Gaea's Cradle is not producing any mana, so Contamination's replacement effect doesn't apply.

question: Aubrey controls a [Necromancy] that was cast during their declare blockers step. During Aubrey's end step, Nikolai activates [Duskmantle Guildmage]'s first ability. Does Aubrey lose 1 life when the Necromancy is sacrificed?
answer:
Yes — Aubrey loses 1 life when Necromancy is put into their graveyard (and another 1 life for the creature card, see below).

Why: Necromancy's own text says "You may cast this spell as though it had flash. If you cast it any time a sorcery couldn't have been cast, the controller of the permanent it becomes sacrifices it at the beginning of the next cleanup step." Aubrey cast Necromancy during their declare blockers step, when a sorcery couldn't be cast, and (assuming they used Necromancy's own flash-granting ability rather than some outside effect — [Necromancy ruling #4]) Necromancy is sacrificed at the beginning of the cleanup step of that same turn.

Duskmantle Guildmage's first ability sets up a delayed triggered ability: "Whenever a card is put into an opponent's graveyard from anywhere this turn, that player loses 1 life" ([Duskmantle Guildmage ruling #0]). Nikolai activated it during Aubrey's end step, so it is active for the remainder of that turn — and the cleanup step is part of that same turn. Aubrey is an opponent of Nikolai, and Necromancy is a card (not a token), so the delayed ability triggers and Aubrey loses 1 life ([Duskmantle Guildmage ruling #1]).

Second loss: Necromancy also says "When this enchantment leaves the battlefield, that creature's controller sacrifices it." If the reanimated creature is an actual card (the normal case, since Necromancy returns a creature card from a graveyard), it too goes to Aubrey's graveyard and triggers the delayed ability again for another 1 life, for 2 total. If that permanent were somehow a token, it would not trigger ([Duskmantle Guildmage ruling #1]).

Timing note: I'm assuming Nikolai's activation resolved during the end step, before the turn reached cleanup. If it somehow didn't resolve before Necromancy was sacrificed, no delayed ability would exist yet and Aubrey would lose no life.

Multiplayer: this works the same at any table size — Duskmantle Guildmage's ability considers each of Nikolai's opponents, not just one ([Duskmantle Guildmage ruling #2]), so Aubrey is covered whether the game has two players or more.

One gap: the provided rules context doesn't include the rules governing the cleanup step itself (how triggered abilities during cleanup are handled and whether players receive priority). That doesn't change whether the life loss happens, only the exact procedural handling of the trigger.

question: Alma casts [Virulent Wound], targeting Nico's [Bronze Sable]. In response, Nico casts [Brute Strength] on the Bronze Sable. What happens at the end of the turn?
answer:
Bronze Sable survives Virulent Wound, but dies as the turn ends, and Nico gets a poison counter.

Step by step (assuming Brute Strength resolves first, since it was cast in response and is on top of the stack):
- Brute Strength resolves: Bronze Sable becomes 5/2 with trample until end of turn.
- Virulent Wound resolves: a -1/-1 counter goes on Bronze Sable, making it 4/1. It isn't destroyed, and Virulent Wound also sets up a delayed trigger for when Bronze Sable dies this turn.
- At end of turn, Brute Strength's +3/+1 wears off. Bronze Sable goes back to its printed 2/1, and the -1/-1 counter (which is permanent) makes it 1/0. A creature with 0 toughness is put into its owner's graveyard.
- Because that still happens during the same turn Virulent Wound resolved, the delayed trigger applies and Nico, as Bronze Sable's controller, gets a poison counter. Virulent Wound's ruling confirms the flip side: had Bronze Sable not gone to the graveyard on that turn, no poison counter would be given.

Note the provided context doesn't include the numbered rules for the cleanup step or for 0-toughness creatures being put into the graveyard, so that part rests on Bronze Sable's printed 2/1 stats plus the Virulent Wound ruling rather than a quoted rule.

If instead you meant that Virulent Wound somehow resolved before Brute Strength, nothing changes: the -1/-1 counter would make Bronze Sable 1/0 and it would die immediately, again giving Nico a poison counter, and Brute Strength would be countered for having an illegal target.

This all works the same at a two-player or multiplayer table; only Nico (Bronze Sable's controller) is affected.

If so, those state-based actions are performed, then those triggered abilities are put on the stack, then the active player gets priority. Players may cast spells and activate abilities. Once the stack is empty and all players pass in succession, another cleanup step begins.

The delayed triggered ability created by Virulent Wound is not a continuous effect, so it still exists during the cleanup step, and will trigger due to Bronze Sable dying. Nico gets a poison counter.

question: Angelina controls [Ice Cauldron]. Noel controls [Suppression Field]. Angelina activates Ice Cauldron's first ability with X=1, paying {C}{C}{C}. On Angelina's next turn, they activate Ice Cauldron's second ability. How much mana do they add?
answer:
Angelina adds {C}{C}{C} — three colorless mana.

Why: Suppression Field says "Activated abilities cost {2} more to activate unless they're mana abilities." Ice Cauldron's first ability isn't a mana ability, so its cost became {X}, {T} plus {2} more. With X=1 that's {1} + {2} = {3} generic, which Angelina paid with {C}{C}{C} (colorless mana is legal for generic costs).

Ice Cauldron notes "the type and amount of mana spent to pay this activation cost" — that's the mana actually spent, all {C}{C}{C}, not the value of X. Ice Cauldron ruling #8 confirms it counts only mana spent and doesn't see X, so the {2} tax mana is noted right along with the rest.

On the later activation of the second ability, Angelina taps Ice Cauldron and removes the charge counter to add {C}{C}{C}, spendable only to cast the last card exiled with Ice Cauldron (Ice Cauldron ruling #13). That second ability is a mana ability (Ice Cauldron ruling #0), so per Suppression Field ruling #0 Suppression Field does not tax it — no extra {2} is required to activate it, and the tax does not reduce the mana produced.

Number of players doesn't matter here: Suppression Field affects activated abilities of all players, so the result is the same in a two-player or multiplayer game.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).

gold_text.602.1a: Activated abilities have a cost and an effect. They are written as “[Cost]: [Effect.] [Activation instructions (if any).]” The activation cost is everything before the colon (:). An ability’s activation cost must be paid by the player who is activating it. The activation cost of an ability that reads “{2}, {T}: You gain 1 life” is two mana of any type plus tapping the permanent that has the ability.
gold_text.602.2b: To activate an ability is to put it onto the stack and pay its costs, so that it will eventually resolve and have its effect. Only an object’s controller (or its owner, if it doesn’t have a controller) can activate its activated ability unless the object specifically says otherwise. Activating an ability follows the steps listed below, in order. If, at any point during the activation of an ability, a player is unable to comply with any of those steps, the activation is illegal; the game returns to the moment before that ability started to be activated (see rule 733, “Handling Illegal Actions”). Announcements and payments can’t be altered after they’ve been made. The remainder of the process for activating an ability is identical to the process for casting a spell listed in rules 601.2b–i. Those rules apply to activating an ability just as they apply to casting a spell. An activated ability’s analog to a spell’s mana cost (as referenced in rule 601.2f) is its activation cost.

answer_gold: Just {C}. The activation cost of Ice Cauldron's first ability is "{X}, {T}". The additional cost imposed by Suppression Field is not part of the activation cost, and the mana spent on it isn't noted when the ability resolves.

question: Ariel activates [Warped Landscape]. Before that resolves Noe casts [Aven Mindcensor]. When Ariel is resolving Warped Landscape's ability, they find [Panglacial Wurm] in the top four cards of their library. Can they cast it?
answer:
Yes — Ariel can cast Panglacial Wurm, but only if they do it before finishing/finding with the search.

Details:

1. Aven Mindcensor's ability changes Ariel's search so that Ariel searches only the top four cards of their library. That is still a search of Ariel's own library ([Aven Mindcensor ruling #0]), and Panglacial Wurm's ability ("While you're searching your library, you may cast this card from your library") works during any effect that tells Ariel to search their own library ([Panglacial Wurm ruling #6]). So the permission is live during the Warped Landscape search.

2. Casting Panglacial Wurm is casting it from the library, not "finding" it, so the top-four restriction on what can be found ([Aven Mindcensor ruling #2]) doesn't stop the cast. Here Panglacial Wurm is in the visible top four anyway.

3. Timing: Ariel must cast Panglacial Wurm before they find any card with the Warped Landscape search ([Panglacial Wurm ruling #1]). Your question says Ariel already "finds" Panglacial Wurm among the top four — I'm reading that as "sees it while looking," with no basic land found yet, so the cast is still legal. If instead Ariel had already announced finding a basic land, the window has closed and Panglacial Wurm can't be cast during that search.

4. Cost and procedure: normal casting rules apply except for timing and zone. Ariel pays {5}{G}{G} plus any additional costs, and may activate mana abilities (which don't use the stack and resolve immediately, [605.3b]) to help pay ([Panglacial Wurm ruling #0]). Panglacial Wurm goes on the stack; Ariel then resumes the Warped Landscape search where they left off, finds a basic land (from the top four only), puts it onto the battlefield tapped, then shuffles ([Aven Mindcensor ruling #1]). A Panglacial Wurm cast this way can't also be found by that search ([Panglacial Wurm ruling #4]).

5. After the Warped Landscape ability finishes resolving, the active player gets priority with Panglacial Wurm on the stack, and any cast triggers go on the stack then ([Panglacial Wurm ruling #3]).

This works the same at a multiplayer table: Aven Mindcensor restricts library searches by each of Noe's opponents, and Panglacial Wurm's permission depends only on Ariel searching Ariel's own library.

gold_text.614.6: If an event is replaced, it never happens. A modified event occurs instead, which may in turn trigger abilities. Note that the modified event may contain instructions that can’t be carried out, in which case the impossible instruction is simply ignored.
gold_text.701.23f: Search If searching a zone is replaced with searching a portion of that zone, any other instructions that refer to searching the zone still apply. Any abilities that trigger on a library being searched will trigger. Aven Mindcensor says, in part, “If an opponent would search a library, that player searches the top four cards of that library instead.” Veteran Explorer says “When this creature dies, each player may search their library for up to two basic land cards, put them onto the battlefield, then shuffle.” An opponent who searched the top four cards of their library because of Veteran Explorer’s ability would shuffle the entire library.

cited_text.605.3b: Activating an activated mana ability follows the rules for activating any other activated ability (see rule 602.2), with the following exceptions: An activated mana ability doesn’t go on the stack, so it can’t be targeted, countered, or otherwise responded to. Rather, it resolves immediately after it is activated. (See rule 405.6c.)

answer_gold: Yes. Aven Mindcensor's ability is a replacement effect that replaces searching a library with searching only the top four cards of that library. However for the purposes of Panglacial Wurm's effect, it still qualifies as "searching a library".

question: Addison has cast a sideboard card from [Glittering Wish], which is now in their graveyard. Addison then restarts the game with [Karn Liberated]. What happens?
answer:
The game restarts under Karn Liberated's −14 ability, and neither Glittering Wish nor the card it fetched stays where it was: the wished sideboard card goes back to Addison's sideboard (it can't be shuffled into the new deck), and Glittering Wish itself, having been exiled or put in the graveyard without being exiled by Karn Liberated, simply becomes part of Addison's shuffled deck again for the new game.

Details:

- Only non-Aura permanent cards exiled with Karn Liberated's first two abilities (+4 and −3) remain in exile when the game restarts; those are put onto the battlefield under Addison's control after the pregame procedure [Karn Liberated ruling #6] [Karn Liberated ruling #4]. Glittering Wish's own text exiles it as part of its effect (and you say it's in the graveyard), so it was not exiled with Karn Liberated and therefore doesn't stay in exile.
- Everything else resets: each player shuffles their whole deck, life totals return to the format's starting total, players draw seven and may mulligan, and Addison — the controller of the ability that restarted the game — is the starting player [Karn Liberated ruling #9]. No counters or emblems carry over [Karn Liberated ruling #10], and nothing that happened in the old game applies [Karn Liberated ruling #1]. The original game just ends with no winner or loser [Karn Liberated ruling #12].
- The wished card: in a tournament, a card chosen "from outside the game" with Glittering Wish must come from the sideboard [Glittering Wish ruling #0]. Since players can't move cards between their deck and sideboard before the new game [Karn Liberated ruling #5], that card is still a sideboard card and returns to Addison's sideboard rather than being shuffled into the new deck. In a casual game where it came from a personal collection, it likewise isn't part of the deck and goes back outside the game. (If Addison had instead exiled that card with Karn Liberated's +4 or −3 and it was a non-Aura permanent card, it would stay in exile and hit the battlefield in the new game.)
- Multiplayer: with more than two players, any player who had already left before the restart isn't in the new game [Karn Liberated ruling #11], and if Addison were to leave the game, permanents Addison controls from Karn Liberated's ability are exiled [Karn Liberated ruling #3]. In a two-player game those caveats simply don't come up.

Assumption on timing: I'm assuming the Glittering Wish and the wished spell both fully resolved before Karn Liberated's −14 was activated. If the wished card were still on the stack or in hand when the restart happened, the result is the same — it isn't exiled by Karn Liberated, so it leaves the game state and returns to the sideboard.

answer_gold: The sideboard card is shuffled into Addison's library for the restarted game.

question: Alvin controls [Mycosynth Lattice], a [Dance of the Dead] attached to a [Streetbreaker Wurm] that it returned to the battlefield, and a [Mizzium Transreliquat] that is currently a copy of [Sakashima of a Thousand Faces] due to its second ability. Alvin casts [Eureka], choosing to put [March of the Machines] onto the battlefield, then putting [Copy Artifact] onto the battlefield, which copies the Mizzium Transreliquat and then copies the Dance of the Dead with its new copy ability. (The one from Sakashima of a Thousand Faces.) They choose for it to enchant a [Viashino Warrior] in their graveyard. As Eureka continues resolving, they put [Shimatsu the Bloodcloaked] onto the battlefield and sacrifice March of the Machines. After Copy Artifact's trigger resolves and returns the Viashino Warrior to the battlefield, Alvin activates the ability of the Copy Artifact to turn it into a copy of Streetbreaker Wurm. What happens?
answer:
Direct answer: the Copy Artifact stops being a Dance of the Dead and becomes a colorless 6/4 artifact creature enchantment named Streetbreaker Wurm that also has the {1}{U}{R} ability. Because it never left the battlefield, Dance of the Dead's "When this Aura leaves the battlefield, that creature's controller sacrifices it" ability does NOT trigger, so the returned Viashino Warrior is not sacrificed — it simply stops being enchanted (the copy is no longer an Aura) and drops from 5/3 back to 4/2. Nothing is sacrificed, and Alvin's original Dance of the Dead and Streetbreaker Wurm are unaffected.

Why each piece works this way:

1) Legality of the targets. Mycosynth Lattice makes every permanent an artifact, so both Dance of the Dead and Streetbreaker Wurm are legal targets for a "target artifact" copy ability. Mycosynth Lattice also lets Alvin pay the {U} and {R} in {1}{U}{R} with mana of any color ({1} is generic and payable with anything) [Mycosynth Lattice ruling #0].

2) What the Copy Artifact was. Copy Artifact entered as a copy of the Mizzium Transreliquat, and copy effects already applying to it are copied [Mizzium Transreliquat ruling #3], so it was a Sakashima of a Thousand Faces with the {1}{U}{R} ability, and an enchantment in addition to its other types [Copy Artifact ruling #2], colorless [Copy Artifact ruling #0, Mycosynth Lattice ruling #2].

3) Timing flag on the Dance of the Dead trigger. Strictly, activated abilities can't be activated during Eureka's resolution, and a permanent that *becomes* a copy of Dance of the Dead doesn't "enter," so Dance of the Dead's enters-the-battlefield trigger (which is what puts the creature card onto the battlefield and attaches the Aura) would never trigger [Dance of the Dead ruling #1]. I'm answering on the premise the question gives me — that the trigger did resolve and Viashino Warrior returned attached. If instead no such trigger happened, Viashino Warrior was never on the battlefield at all and the only result of the last activation is that the Copy Artifact becomes a 6/4 Streetbreaker Wurm copy.

4) Why nothing died to March of the Machines. While March of the Machines was on the battlefield, Mycosynth Lattice made Dance of the Dead a noncreature artifact, so March of the Machines turned it into a 2/2 artifact creature Aura, which can't enchant anything and would be unattached and then put into its owner's graveyard — as *state-based actions* [Mycosynth Lattice ruling #3, March of the Machines ruling #0]. Those checks only happen when a player would receive priority, and March of the Machines was already sacrificed to Shimatsu the Bloodcloaked before Eureka finished resolving [Eureka ruling #3]. So Dance of the Dead stayed attached and Streetbreaker Wurm was never sacrificed.

5) The new copy's characteristics. The last copy effect to resolve overwrites the previous one, and because the ability says "except it has this ability," the Copy Artifact keeps only the {1}{U}{R} ability — Sakashima's "legend rule doesn't apply" and partner abilities are gone [Mizzium Transreliquat rulings #0 and #2, Sakashima of a Thousand Faces ruling #9]. Alvin's Mizzium Transreliquat is still a Sakashima copy, so the legend rule still doesn't apply to Alvin's permanents [Sakashima of a Thousand Faces ruling #6]; if that ever stops, duplicate legends would have to be culled [Sakashima of a Thousand Faces ruling #2]. Copiable values are printed values as modified by copy effects only — so the copy is 6/4, not 7/5; the original Streetbreaker Wurm's +1/+1 from Dance of the Dead is a layer 7 power/toughness effect applied after copy effects and is not copied [Mizzium Transreliquat ruling #1, 613.1g]. The copy is also still an enchantment [Copy Artifact ruling #2], and since it isn't an Aura anymore it stays on the battlefield attached to nothing. It has summoning sickness for attacking/{T} abilities this turn [March of the Machines ruling #4].

Player count: nothing here changes between two players and a multiplayer table; Eureka's loop just runs through however many players are in the game [Eureka ruling #3].

question: Aspen controls a [Blood Tyrant] that they took control of from Briella using [Malevolent Whispers]. Aspen has 1 life. Cason casts [Volt Charge] targeting Aspen. After it resolves and Aspen loses the game, will Blood Tyrant get the +1/+1 counters?
answer:
Yes — Blood Tyrant's third ability does trigger, but whether the counters actually land isn't fully settled by the rules I was given.

What's clear: Volt Charge deals 3 damage to Aspen, who is at 1 life, so Aspen's life total drops to 0 or less and Aspen loses the game as a state-based action. Blood Tyrant's third ability reads "Whenever a player loses the game, put five +1/+1 counters on this creature," and [Blood Tyrant ruling #1] confirms it triggers no matter how a player loses the game, including by having a life total of 0 or less. So the trigger event happens and the ability triggers.

Assumed timing: I'm assuming Aspen loses the game only after Volt Charge finishes resolving (as you stated), so Blood Tyrant is still on the battlefield under Aspen's control when the loss occurs and the ability triggers. If instead Blood Tyrant had already left the battlefield before the loss, there would be no permanent with the ability to trigger.

What the provided rules don't cover: they contain nothing about what happens when a player leaves the game — i.e., whether Malevolent Whispers' "gain control of target creature until end of turn" effect ends and Blood Tyrant returns to Briella, what happens to objects Aspen controlled, and whether a trigger controlled by a departing player is removed from the stack before it resolves. I can't ground that part in the context, so I won't guess whether the five counters ultimately get placed.

Player count matters: this scenario names three players (Aspen, Briella, Cason), so the game continues after Aspen loses and the trigger has something to do. In a strictly two‑player game, one player losing ends the game immediately, and counters would be irrelevant. The provided context doesn't include the specific multiplayer "leaves the game" rules, so treat that distinction as general framing rather than a cited rule.

Side note: Volt Charge also proliferates, and per [Volt Charge ruling #2] Cason chooses any number (including zero) of permanents/players, so Cason is under no obligation to add a counter to Blood Tyrant; per [Volt Charge ruling #6] that choice is made on resolution and can't be responded to afterward.

The list of exceptions is as follows:

However, some triggered abilities are exceptions to this rule; the game “looks back in time” to determine if those abilities trigger, using the existence of those abilities and the appearance of objects immediately prior to the event. The list of exceptions is as follows: Abilities that trigger when a player loses the game look back in time.

Then, if that player controlled any objects on the stack not represented by cards, those objects cease to exist. Then, if there are any objects still controlled by that player, those objects are exiled. This is not a state-based action. It happens as soon as the player leaves the game. If the player who left the game had priority at the time they left, priority passes to the next player in turn order who’s still in the game. Alex casts Mind Control, an Aura that reads, “You control enchanted creature,” on Bianca’s Assault Griffin. If Alex leaves the game, so does Mind Control, and Assault Griffin reverts to Bianca’s control. If, instead, Bianca leaves the game, so does Assault Griffin, and Mind Control is put into Alex’s graveyard. Alex casts Act of Treason, which reads, in part, “Gain control of target creature until end of turn,” targeting Bianca’s Runeclaw Bears. If Alex leaves the game, Act of Treason’s change-of-control effect ends and Runeclaw Bears reverts to Bianca’s control. Alex casts Bribery, which reads, “Search target opponent’s library for a creature card and put that card onto the battlefield under your control. Then that player shuffles their library,” targeting Bianca. Alex puts Serra Angel onto the battlefield from Bianca’s library. If Bianca leaves the game, Serra Angel also leaves the game. If, instead, Alex leaves the game, Serra Angel is exiled. Alex controls Genesis Chamber, which reads, “Whenever a nontoken creature enters, if Genesis Chamber is untapped, that creature’s controller creates a 1/1 colorless Myr artifact creature token.” If Alex leaves the game, all such Myr tokens that entered the battlefield under Alex’s control leave the game, and all such Myr tokens that entered the battlefield under any other player’s control remain in the game.

If an object that would be owned by a player who has left the game would be created in any zone, it isn’t created. If a triggered ability that would be controlled by a player who has left the game would be put onto the stack, it isn’t put on the stack. Astral Slide is an enchantment that reads, “Whenever a player cycles a card, you may exile target creature. If you do, return that creature to the battlefield under its owner’s control at the beginning of the next end step.” During Alex’s turn, Bianca uses Astral Slide’s ability to exile Alex’s Hypnotic Specter. Before the end of that turn, Bianca leaves the game. At the beginning of the end step, the delayed triggered ability generated by Astral Slide that would return Hypnotic Specter to the battlefield triggers, but it isn’t put on the stack. Hypnotic Specter never returns to the battlefield.

answer_gold: No. As Aspen loses the game, the effect granting them control of Blood Tyrant ends, and it returns to Briella. "Loses the game" triggers use the game state immediately before they triggered to determine how that trigger is handled. Since Aspen controlled Blood Tyrant right before losing the game, the trigger would be placed onto the stack under their control. However Aspen is no longer in the game when the trigger would be placed onto the stack, so it never is.

question: Aspen, Brycen, and Collins begin a multiplayer game. In Aspen's upkeep, they use [Leyline of Anticipation], several [Simian Spirit Guide]s and [Desperate Ritual]s, and [Goblin Charbelcher] to kill Brycen. Does Aspen draw a card for the turn?
answer:
The provided rules don't settle this. Nothing in the context covers the draw step, the turn structure of the first turn, or whether the starting player in a multiplayer game skips their first draw — the closest turn-structure rules given here are only about putting lore counters on Sagas at the start of the precombat main phase [505.4] [714.3c], which is irrelevant to drawing.

question: Addison, Brixton, and Collins started playing a multiplayer game. Collins lost the game, and then Addison restarted the game with [Karn Liberated]. Will Addison draw a card on the first turn of the restarted game?
answer:
No — Addison won't draw on the first turn of the restarted game (aside from the opening hand of seven).

Why: Karn Liberated's −14 restarts the game, and Collins, having already left before the restart, is not part of the new game [Karn Liberated ruling #11]. That leaves just Addison and Brixton, so the restarted game is a two-player game. The new game begins like any normal game: each player shuffles (except cards left in exile by Karn Liberated), life totals reset to the format's starting total, players draw seven and may mulligan [Karn Liberated ruling #9]. Addison, who controlled the ability that restarted the game, is the starting player in the new game [Karn Liberated ruling #9]. In a two-player game the starting player skips the draw step of their first turn, so Addison draws nothing on turn one.

Caveat on grounding: the rule that the starting player skips their first draw step in a two-player game is not among the rules provided to me, so that specific part rests on the fact that the restarted game "starts like a game normally does" per [Karn Liberated ruling #9] rather than on a quoted rule. What the provided material does settle firmly is that (a) Addison is the starting player and (b) Collins is not in the new game, so the table is two players rather than three. Had Collins still been in the game at the time of the restart, the game would have been a three-player game, where the starting player does not skip their first draw — but again, that multiplayer draw rule isn't in the provided context.

Also note: after the pregame procedure but before the first turn, Karn Liberated's ability finishes resolving and the exiled non-Aura permanent cards enter the battlefield under Addison's control; any resulting triggers go on the stack at the beginning of the first upkeep step [Karn Liberated ruling #4].

question: Aniyah casts [Martyrdom], targeting their [Douser of Lights]. After it resolves, Nico takes control of Douser of Lights with [Act of Aggression]. Can Nico activate the ability it gained from Martyrdom?
answer:
No. Nico cannot activate the granted ability. Martyrdom's granted ability reads "{0}: The next 1 damage that would be dealt to target creature, planeswalker, or player this turn is dealt to this creature instead," and Martyrdom explicitly adds "Only you may activate this ability." The "you" in that restriction is Aniyah, the controller of the Martyrdom spell that created the effect — not whoever happens to control Douser of Lights at the time. So even though Act of Aggression gives Nico control of Douser of Lights (untapped, with haste) until end of turn, Aniyah remains the only player who may activate the {0} ability, and Aniyah may still do so while Nico controls Douser of Lights.

Note also that Act of Aggression's control change doesn't move or remove Auras or Equipment (Act of Aggression ruling #6) and doesn't strip abilities granted by Martyrdom; the ability lasts until end of turn as printed.

This is a card-text answer: Martyrdom's own "Only you may activate this ability" clause overrides the general expectation that a permanent's controller activates its abilities. The provided rules context contains only prevention/damage-replacement rules (Martyrdom's redirection is a replacement of the damage event, not a prevention effect — see the framework in 615.1a and 120.4c/120.4d for how damage events get modified before they occur), and nothing in it changes who may activate the ability. Nothing here differs between a two-player game and a multiplayer table: only Aniyah may activate it in either case.

question: Ashley has restarted the game with a [Karn Liberated] that exiled an [Ajani's Chosen]. Ashley chooses to begin the restarted game with a [Leyline of Anticipation] on the battlefield. Does Ajani's Chosen trigger?
answer:
No — Ajani's Chosen doesn't trigger off that Leyline of Anticipation.

Sequence: the restarted game begins with the normal pregame procedure — shuffle, life totals, draw seven, mulligans — and then players may take actions from their opening hands, such as putting Leyline of Anticipation onto the battlefield [Karn Liberated ruling #9], [Leyline of Anticipation ruling #0]. Only after the pregame procedure is complete, but still before the new game's first turn, does Karn Liberated's ability finish resolving and put the exiled cards (here Ajani's Chosen) onto the battlefield [Karn Liberated ruling #4].

So when Leyline of Anticipation enters the battlefield, Ajani's Chosen is still in exile and has no ability on the battlefield to trigger. Ajani's Chosen only triggers when an enchantment you control enters while Ajani's Chosen is already on the battlefield [Ajani's Chosen ruling #3].

For contrast: if some other enchantment you control entered later, during the new game, Ajani's Chosen would trigger normally, and note that any triggers caused by Karn Liberated putting permanents onto the battlefield are put onto the stack at the beginning of the first upkeep step [Karn Liberated ruling #4].

Multiplayer note: this timing is the same regardless of player count; the only multiplayer difference is that any player who had already left before the restart isn't in the new game [Karn Liberated ruling #11], and opening-hand actions are taken by the starting player first, then each other player in turn order [Leyline of Anticipation ruling #0].

question: Nehemiah controls a [Skullbriar, the Walking Grave] with 2 +1/+1 counters on it. Ari casts [Bishop of Binding], exiling the Skullbriar, the Walking Grave. When Ari attacks with Bishop of Binding on their next turn, what will X equal in Bishop of Binding's triggered ability?
answer:
X = 3.

Skullbriar, the Walking Grave has the ability "Counters remain on Skullbriar as it moves to any zone other than a player's hand or library." Exile is not a hand or library, so the two +1/+1 counters stay on the Skullbriar, the Walking Grave card in exile. This specific card text overrides the general behavior described in [Bishop of Binding ruling #1], which says counters on the exiled creature cease to exist — that ruling covers ordinary creatures, but Skullbriar, the Walking Grave's own printed text wins.

Counters that modify power/toughness apply to Skullbriar, the Walking Grave even outside the battlefield ([Skullbriar, the Walking Grave ruling #2]), so the exiled card is 3/3 — base 1/1 plus two +1/+1 counters. Bishop of Binding's attack trigger sets X to the power of the exiled card, measured only as that ability resolves ([Bishop of Binding ruling #5]), so the targeted Vampire gets +3/+3 until end of turn.

One caveat: if Bishop of Binding has left the battlefield while the attack trigger is on the stack (so there's no exiled card at resolution), X would be 0 instead ([Bishop of Binding ruling #0]). This answer doesn't depend on player count — it works the same at a two-player table or in multiplayer, though in multiplayer the exile target must be a creature an opponent of Ari controls.

question: Neriah controls a [Containment Priest] and has a [Knotvine Mystic] in their graveyard. Alan casts [Ghastly Conscription], targeting Neriah. What happens to the Knotvine Mystic?
answer:
The Knotvine Mystic never gets onto the battlefield — Containment Priest exiles it instead, and it stays in exile.

Why: Ghastly Conscription exiles all creature cards from Neriah's graveyard face down, shuffles them, then manifests them, i.e. puts them onto the battlefield face down as 2/2 creatures (a manifested permanent is a 2/2 colorless creature with no name, mana cost, or abilities — [Ghastly Conscription ruling #8]). Knotvine Mystic is therefore a nontoken creature that would enter the battlefield without having been cast, which is exactly what Containment Priest's replacement ability catches ("If a nontoken creature would enter and it wasn't cast, exile it instead"). Manifesting is not casting, so the exception for cast creatures ([Containment Priest ruling #1]) doesn't help. The fact that it's entering face down as a creature is enough — what matters is that it's entering as a creature ([Containment Priest ruling #3]).

Practical result: Knotvine Mystic simply ends up in exile rather than on the battlefield, and Alan controls no manifested Knotvine Mystic. The same happens to every other creature card Ghastly Conscription tried to manifest from Neriah's graveyard while Containment Priest is on the battlefield. Since the manifested cards would have entered under Alan's control face down, note that a face-down permanent that leaves the battlefield must be revealed ([Ghastly Conscription ruling #11]) — but here Knotvine Mystic never actually entered the battlefield, so it's just exiled from the face-down pile; players may or may not learn its identity depending on how it was handled, though nothing hides it once it's exiled by a replacement effect rather than put onto the battlefield.

Multiplayer: nothing changes. Containment Priest's ability applies to any creature entering the battlefield, no matter whose it is and no matter how many players are in the game; Ghastly Conscription just needs a target player, so the answer is the same in a two-player or multiplayer game.

question: Avery controls [Magnetic Web] and is attacking with two [Leatherback Baloth]s with magnet counters on them. Nayeli controls one [Imperial Moth] that also has a magnet counter on it. What are Nayeli's legal blocks?
answer:
Nayeli must block with Imperial Moth, and it may block either one of the two Leatherback Baloths — her choice. It cannot block both, and declining to block at all is not legal.

Why: Magnetic Web reads "Whenever a creature with a magnet counter on it attacks, all creatures with magnet counters on them block that creature this turn if able." Both Leatherback Baloths have magnet counters and are attacking, so the ability triggers twice, creating two separate blocking requirements on Nayeli's Imperial Moth (which has a magnet counter). A single creature can only be declared as a blocker for one attacking creature, so both requirements cannot be met at once. Each requirement says "if able," so Imperial Moth blocks one of the two Leatherback Baloths, satisfying as many requirements as it can — blocking either Leatherback Baloth is equally legal, and blocking neither would satisfy zero requirements when one could be satisfied. Note Imperial Moth is a 2/4 enchantment creature with flying; flying doesn't stop it from blocking a nonflying Leatherback Baloth.

One caveat on grounding: the general rules text for how blocking requirements and restrictions are evaluated (the "maximum possible number of requirements" rule, 509.1c) was not included in my rules context, so the "block one, your choice" conclusion above rests on Magnetic Web's own "if able" wording rather than a quoted numbered rule.

Multiplayer: this analysis is the same whether the game is two-player or multiplayer, except that in a multiplayer game only the creatures controlled by the chosen defending player (here Nayeli, if she is the defending player being attacked) are required to block; Magnetic Web's requirement can't force a creature controlled by a player who isn't the defending player for that attack to block. No multiplayer combat rules were provided in my context, so treat that last point as a practical note rather than a cited rule.

question: Arden controls [Naga Vitalist] and a [Deathrite Shaman] that's currently a land due to [Xenograft] (naming "Saproling") and [Life and Limb]. Neither player has any land cards in their graveyards. If Arden taps Naga Vitalist, what type(s) of mana can it produce?
answer:
Arden can tap Naga Vitalist for one mana of any color — {W}, {U}, {B}, {R}, or {G} — even though no land cards are in any graveyard.

Why: Xenograft (naming Saproling) makes each creature Arden controls a Saproling in addition to its other types, so Deathrite Shaman is a Saproling. Life and Limb then makes all Saprolings 1/1 green Saproling creatures and Forest lands in addition to their other types, so Deathrite Shaman is now a land (a Forest) that keeps all of its own abilities [Life and Limb ruling #3].

As a Forest it has "{T}: Add {G}" [Life and Limb ruling #2], and it still has its own first ability, "{T}: Exile target land card from a graveyard. Add one mana of any color." Naga Vitalist adds one mana of any type that a land Arden controls *could* produce, and it checks the effects of all mana-producing abilities of those lands without checking their costs, targets, or legality [Naga Vitalist ruling #0] and without caring about restrictions or riders [Naga Vitalist ruling #3]. So the empty graveyards don't matter — the "any color" effect of Deathrite Shaman's ability is still visible to Naga Vitalist. That's true even though Deathrite Shaman's first ability isn't a mana ability [Deathrite Shaman ruling #1]; Naga Vitalist only cares that it's an ability that produces mana.

The types of mana are white, blue, black, red, green, and colorless [Naga Vitalist ruling #2]. Colorless {C} is not available from what's described here — it would only be an option if some other land Arden controls could produce colorless mana. Note also that {C} is never interchangeable with generic {N}.

This answer doesn't depend on the number of players; nothing here references opponents' permanents (the graveyard condition is ignored regardless of whose graveyard it is).

question: Adelyn controls [Panharmonicon] and [Mycosynth Lattice] and has [Dwarven Trader] and [Staunch Shieldmate] in their graveyard. They cast [Animate Dead] targeting Dwarven Trader. What happens as it enters the battlefield?
answer:
Animate Dead's enters-the-battlefield triggered ability triggers twice instead of once, but only the first instance actually does anything: Dwarven Trader comes back to the battlefield under Adelyn's control with Animate Dead attached to it. The second instance resolves and does nothing further — Staunch Shieldmate stays in the graveyard.

Why it triggers twice: Panharmonicon says that if an artifact or creature entering causes a triggered ability of a permanent you control to trigger, that ability triggers an additional time, and it applies to a permanent's own enters-the-battlefield triggers, which start with "when" or "whenever" [Panharmonicon ruling #4]. Normally an Aura entering wouldn't qualify, but Mycosynth Lattice makes all permanents artifacts in addition to their other types, so Animate Dead is an artifact Aura as it enters [Mycosynth Lattice ruling #1], satisfying Panharmonicon. Adelyn controls the permanent with the ability, which is all Panharmonicon requires [Panharmonicon ruling #3].

First instance resolves: the intervening "if" clause ("if it's on the battlefield") is checked both on triggering and on resolution [Intervening "If" Clause]; Animate Dead is there, so it loses "enchant creature card in a graveyard," gains "enchant creature put onto the battlefield with this Aura," returns Dwarven Trader to the battlefield under Adelyn's control, and attaches to it [Animate Dead ruling #1]. Dwarven Trader gets -1/-0, so it's a 0/1, and under Mycosynth Lattice it's a colorless artifact creature (so no protection-from-black snag) [Mycosynth Lattice ruling #2, Animate Dead ruling #0].

Second instance resolves: Animate Dead is still on the battlefield, so the condition is met, but its enchant ability is already changed and the enchanted object is now a creature permanent, not a creature card in a graveyard, so there is no "enchanted creature card" to return. Animate Dead also can't be moved to a different creature [Animate Dead ruling #3], and it can't reach Staunch Shieldmate — the target was chosen when the spell was cast and Panharmonicon doesn't copy the spell or let you re-target it; choices for each instance are made separately but there's nothing to choose here [Panharmonicon ruling #8]. Note also that each resolution creates the delayed "when this Aura leaves the battlefield, that creature's controller sacrifices it" trigger; when Animate Dead eventually leaves, Dwarven Trader is sacrificed (the second such trigger finds nothing to do).

This answer is the same regardless of how many players are at the table — nothing here depends on opponents or turn order.

question: Armani controls a [Gaea's Liege] and 3 [Canopy Vista]s. Nico controls a [Reverence] and 1 Canopy Vista. Can Armani attack with the Gaea's Liege?
answer:
Yes — Armani can attack Nico with Gaea's Liege.

Reverence says "Creatures with power 2 or less can't attack you," an attack restriction that's checked when attackers are declared. Per [Gaea's Liege ruling #0], when Gaea's Liege is being declared as an attacker you use its "not attacking" power and toughness; the switch to the attacking characteristic-defining ability only happens after declaration is complete. Armani controls 3 Canopy Vistas, and Canopy Vista has the land type Forest on its type line, so it counts as a Forest for Gaea's Liege even though it isn't a *basic* Forest ([Canopy Vista ruling #0], [Canopy Vista ruling #1]). So at declaration Gaea's Liege is 3/3 — power greater than 2 — and Reverence doesn't stop it.

After the declaration is complete, Gaea's Liege becomes attacking and its power/toughness become the number of Forests the defending player (Nico) controls: 1 Canopy Vista, so Gaea's Liege becomes 1/1. Reverence does not retroactively remove it from combat, because its restriction only applies to the act of declaring an attack, not to a creature already attacking.

One alternative target worth noting: per [Reverence ruling #0], even a creature that can't attack Nico could still attack a planeswalker Nico controls.

Multiplayer note: the provided rules and card text don't change this for a larger table — the answer is the same whether it's a two-player game or more. Just be aware that with more than two players, Gaea's Liege's attacking power/toughness depends on which player (or which player's planeswalker/battle) it's attacking, since it counts Forests the *defending player* controls; against a defender with 3 or more Forests it would be bigger, against one with none it would be 0/0 and die.

question: Ariel attacks with [Wildfire Eternal], which isn't blocked. As the trigger resolves, can they choose to suspend [Charnel Serenade]?
answer:
No. The Wildfire Eternal trigger only lets Ariel cast an instant or sorcery spell from their hand without paying its mana cost — and exiling a card with suspend is not casting it (it doesn't even use the stack), so it isn't something the Wildfire Eternal ability grants permission to do [Charnel Serenade ruling #15].

On top of that, suspend can only be used at a time when Ariel could actually cast the card [Charnel Serenade ruling #10]. Charnel Serenade is a sorcery, so outside of some effect granting flash-like timing, Ariel couldn't use suspend during the declare blockers step anyway.

What Ariel *can* do is use the Wildfire Eternal trigger to cast Charnel Serenade itself from hand for free. Wildfire Eternal's trigger resolves in the declare blockers step, before combat damage, and it explicitly allows casting a sorcery at that time [Wildfire Eternal ruling #0]. Cast that way, Ariel doesn't pay {4}{B}{B}, but can't substitute the {2}{B} suspend cost either, since a card cast "without paying its mana cost" can't be cast for an alternative cost — only mandatory/optional additional costs may be paid [Wildfire Eternal ruling #6], [Charnel Serenade ruling #4]. Resolving Charnel Serenade normally: surveil 3, return a creature card from the graveyard with a finality counter, then exile Charnel Serenade with three time counters, so it will be suspended after resolution and castable again later [Charnel Serenade ruling #1].

This answer doesn't depend on player count; in a multiplayer game the only difference is which player is the defending player for Wildfire Eternal's combat abilities [Wildfire Eternal ruling #7].

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).

The second and third are triggered abilities that function in the exile zone. “Suspend N—[cost]” means “If you could begin to cast this card by putting it onto the stack from your hand, you may pay [cost] and exile it with N time counters on it. This action doesn’t use the stack,” and “At the beginning of your upkeep, if this card is suspended, remove a time counter from it,” and “When the last time counter is removed from this card, if it’s exiled, you may play it without paying its mana cost if able. If you don’t, it remains exiled. If you cast a creature spell this way, it gains haste until you lose control of the spell or the permanent it becomes.”

answer_gold:
Yes. The suspend special action can be taken whenever Charnel Serenade could be cast from Ariel's hand. Normally that's only when Ariel has priority on their turn with an empty stack, but in this case the effect of Wildfire Eternal is letting that happen while the ability resolves.

(They still have to pay the suspend cost, and afterwards they can choose to cast a different spell from hand without paying its mana cost.)

question: Brynn has 1 life and controls a phased-out [Fairgrounds Warden] that exiled Coleman's [Alpha Tyrranax]. Aspen casts [Psychic Purge], targeting Brynn. What happens as Brynn loses the game?
answer:
Coleman gets Alpha Tyrranax back on the battlefield.

Step by step:

1. Psychic Purge deals 1 damage to Brynn, dropping Brynn to 0 life, and Brynn loses the game and leaves the table. (Note Psychic Purge's second ability is about being discarded, which isn't happening here.)

2. When Brynn leaves the game, Brynn's permanents — including the phased-out Fairgrounds Warden — leave the battlefield. Phasing only makes a permanent be treated as though it doesn't exist; it is still on the battlefield until Brynn departs, so its departure satisfies the "until this creature leaves the battlefield" condition in Fairgrounds Warden's exile effect.

3. That creates the second one-shot effect that returns the exiled card, and it returns immediately after Fairgrounds Warden leaves the battlefield, with nothing (not even state-based actions) happening in between [Fairgrounds Warden ruling #2]. Crucially, this return is not a triggered ability that uses the stack, so it does not cease to exist along with the leaving player's spells and abilities [Fairgrounds Warden ruling #0].

4. Alpha Tyrranax returns under its owner's control, i.e. Coleman's control [610.3c].

Details worth knowing: Alpha Tyrranax comes back with no counters, and any Auras that had been attached to it before exile are already in their owners' graveyards [Fairgrounds Warden ruling #4]. Rule 800.4d's "objects owned by a departed player aren't created / their triggered abilities aren't put on the stack" restriction doesn't stop this, because Alpha Tyrranax is Coleman's card and the return isn't a stack ability.

This is inherently a multiplayer answer (three players are involved). In a strict two-player game there would be no "game continues after a player leaves" scenario — the game would simply end when Brynn lost, so the return would be moot.

Timing assumption: I'm assuming Psychic Purge resolves and Brynn hits 0 life with Fairgrounds Warden still phased out on the battlefield. If instead Fairgrounds Warden had already left the battlefield earlier (or if Fairgrounds Warden left before its enters-trigger resolved, so Alpha Tyrranax was never exiled at all), Alpha Tyrranax would have returned at that earlier moment or never been exiled [Fairgrounds Warden ruling #3].

question: Avery controls [Caelorna, Coral Tyrant] and [Darksteel Garrison] that's fortifying [Spire Garden]. Avery casts [Bludgeon Brawl]. After that resolves they activate Darksteel Garrison's equip ability targeting Caelorna, Coral Tyrant. What does the battlefield look like after that ability has resolved and state-based actions have been checked?
answer:
After the equip ability resolves, Darksteel Garrison is attached to Caelorna, Coral Tyrant (no longer fortifying Spire Garden), Caelorna, Coral Tyrant is a 2/8, and Spire Garden is just an ordinary untapped-or-tapped land with no indestructible.

Why:

1. Bludgeon Brawl makes each noncreature, non-Equipment artifact an Equipment with equip {X} and "Equipped creature gets +X/+0," where X is that artifact's mana value. Darksteel Garrison is a noncreature artifact — Fortification, not Equipment — so it becomes an Equipment with equip {2} and "Equipped creature gets +2/+0" (its mana value is 2). It keeps its other types and abilities [Bludgeon Brawl ruling #0], so it is still a Fortification with fortify {3} and its two printed abilities.

2. Activating equip {2} targeting Caelorna, Coral Tyrant attaches Darksteel Garrison to Caelorna, Coral Tyrant. A permanent can only be attached to one object, so it becomes unattached from Spire Garden; Darksteel Garrison itself stays on the battlefield. Caelorna, Coral Tyrant is 0/8 base and gets +2/+0 from the granted Equipment ability, making it 2/8.

3. Darksteel Garrison's own abilities now do nothing: there is no fortified land, so "Fortified land has indestructible" grants nothing and "Whenever fortified land becomes tapped" can't trigger. Spire Garden therefore loses indestructible and tapping it for {R} or {G} no longer pumps anything. (Darksteel Garrison ruling #3, about Darksteel Garrison and the fortified land being destroyed together, is likewise moot now that nothing is fortified.) Fortifications otherwise follow the same rules as Equipment [Darksteel Garrison ruling #2].

4. State-based actions find nothing wrong: Darksteel Garrison as an Equipment is legally attached to a creature, and it is not itself a creature, so the restriction that a creature Equipment can't be equipped to anything doesn't apply [Bludgeon Brawl ruling #3].

Two caveats worth naming: if Bludgeon Brawl later leaves the battlefield (or Darksteel Garrison somehow becomes a creature), Darksteel Garrison stops being an Equipment, becomes unattached from Caelorna, Coral Tyrant, and remains on the battlefield [Bludgeon Brawl ruling #2] — it does not snap back onto Spire Garden. And Spire Garden's own "enters tapped unless you have two or more opponents" clause only mattered when it entered; whether it entered tapped depends on Avery having two or more opponents [Spire Garden ruling #0], but that has no bearing on this equip.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).

Counters, stickers, effects, and damage marked on the object remain with it, even if they are meaningless to the new card type. Similarly, when an effect sets one or more of an object’s subtypes, the new subtype(s) replaces any existing subtypes from the appropriate set (creature types, land types, artifact types, enchantment types, planeswalker types, or spell types). If an object’s card type is removed, the subtypes correlated with that card type will remain if they are also the subtypes of a card type the object currently has; otherwise, they are also removed for the entire time the object’s card type is removed. Removing an object’s subtype doesn’t affect its card types at all.

Darksteel Garrison is attached to Caelorna, Coral Tyrant and not to Spire Garden.

Bludgeon Brawl doesn't specify that the permanents it affects keep their original subtypes, so they are overwritten. This means that Darksteel Garrison ceases to be a Fortification as soon as Bludgeon Brawl enters the battlefield. It will become unattached the next time state-based actions are performed. When its equip ability resolves, it becomes attached to Caelorna, Coral Tyrant.

question: Abel attacks with [Pristine Angel]. While it's tapped, Nico activates [Cephalid Snitch]'s ability targeting Pristine Angel. After that resolves, Abel casts a spell and untaps Pristine Angel. Can Nico now target the Pristine Angel with [Murder]?
answer:
Yes — Nico can target Pristine Angel with Murder, and it will be destroyed (assuming Cephalid Snitch's ability resolved this same turn, which it did).

Why: Pristine Angel's static ability reads "As long as this creature is untapped, it has protection from artifacts and from each color." While Pristine Angel was tapped and attacking it had no protection at all, so Cephalid Snitch's ability ("Sacrifice this creature: Target creature loses protection from black until end of turn") legally targeted it and resolved. That effect lasts until end of turn and keeps stripping protection from black from Pristine Angel even after Pristine Angel untaps and its static ability would otherwise grant protection from each color again — the Snitch effect's later timestamp means the removal applies on top of what the static ability grants. So for the rest of this turn Pristine Angel has flying and protection from artifacts and from white, blue, red, and green, but not from black.

Protection from black is what would normally stop Murder (a black instant) from targeting Pristine Angel; with that protection gone, Murder targets legally and destroys the 4/4 Angel (Pristine Angel has no indestructible or regeneration).

Timing note: I'm assuming Cephalid Snitch's ability fully resolved before Pristine Angel untapped, as described. If instead Pristine Angel had already been untapped and had protection from each color at the time Nico tried to activate Cephalid Snitch's ability targeting it, that activation could not have targeted Pristine Angel in the first place, and Murder would likewise be unable to target it.

Also note Abel casting a spell only triggers Pristine Angel's "Whenever you cast a spell, you may untap this creature" — untapping restores protection from artifacts and the other colors, but it does not undo the until-end-of-turn loss of protection from black. Nico targeting Abel's Pristine Angel with Cephalid Snitch's ability and with Murder each count as committing a crime, if any card cares.

The number of players doesn't change any of this; the provided rules on crime speak of "an opponent," so it works the same at a two-player or multiplayer table.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).

If the effect that created the ability has the later timestamp and the object the ability is on receives a new timestamp, each continuous effect generated by static abilities of that object receives a new timestamp as well, but the relative order of those timestamps remains the same. answer_gold:
Yes. "Protection from all colors" is shorthand for protection from each color individually. It loses protection from black, and still has protection from all the other colors.

(The timestamp of Pristine Angel's ability does not change when it becomes untapped.)

question: Adelyn controls [Back from the Brink] and has [Shifting Wall] in their graveyard. Can Adelyn activate Back from the Brink's ability to create a token of Shifting Wall? Can they pay more than {0} to do so? If so, will it enter the battlefield with any +1/+1 counters?
answer:
Yes, Adelyn can activate Back from the Brink's ability exiling Shifting Wall from their graveyard, but the mana cost they pay is {0}, and the Shifting Wall token enters with no +1/+1 counters — so it's a 0/0 and is put into the graveyard immediately as a state-based action.

Why: Back from the Brink says "Exile a creature card from your graveyard and pay its mana cost." Shifting Wall's mana cost is {X}, and when a card's mana cost containing {X} is paid this way, X is considered to be zero [Back from the Brink ruling #3]. Adelyn cannot choose a larger value for X to pay more, because Adelyn isn't casting Shifting Wall — no X is announced, and cost-affecting rules for casting don't apply here [Back from the Brink ruling #1].

Shifting Wall's "This creature enters with X +1/+1 counters on it" is an "enters with" replacement ability, which does function for the token [Back from the Brink ruling #2], but with X = 0 it gives zero counters. The token is therefore a 0/0 Wall with defender, meaning it also could never attack [702.3b].

Timing note: the ability is "Activate only as a sorcery," so Adelyn must do this during their own main phase with an empty stack. Nothing here depends on the number of players — the answer is the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table.

In that case, the value of X is the value chosen or determined for it as the spell was cast.
